work: Enarratio in Epistolam catholicam B. Jacobi
source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. XIII (Montreuil)

1.title: EXPOSITIO PRIMI CAPITULI : JACOBUS, DEI ET DOMINI NOSTRI JESU CHRISTI SERVUS.
1.title_en: Exposition of the first chapter: James, the servant of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ.

paras.t: JACOBUS, Dei et Domini nostri Jesu Christi servus. Iste Jacobus est, respectu alterius Jacobi apostoli, Minor vocatus : Minor, inquam, vocatione ad apostolatum, non sanctitate et perfectione virtutum. De hujus enim Jacobi miranda atque præcipua sanctitate, in ejus Legenda multa leguntur, et de eo in Actibus Apostolorum frequenter fit mentio. Erat siquidem primus Jerosolymitarum Christianorum episcopus. Eratque excellentiæ tantæ, ut Paulus dicat apostolus : Jacobus, Cephas (qui et Petrus) et Joannes, qui videbantur columnæ esse, dexteras dederunt mihi et Barnabæ societatis, ut nos in gentibus, ipsi autem in circumcisione evangelizarent.
paras.en: [[1:1|James, the servant of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ|JACOBUS, Dei et Domini nostri Jesu Christi servus]]. This James is the one called the Less, in respect of the other apostle James: the Less, I say, in his calling to the apostolate, not in holiness and the perfection of the virtues. For many things are read in his Legend of this James's wonderful and surpassing holiness, and he is often mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles. He was indeed the first bishop of the Christians of Jerusalem. And he was of such eminence that Paul the Apostle says: [[Gal 2:9|James and Cephas|Jacobus, Cephas]] (who is also Peter) [[Gal 2:9|and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship|et Joannes, qui videbantur columnæ esse, dexteras dederunt mihi et Barnabæ societatis]], [[Gal 2:9|that we should go unto the Gentiles, and they unto the circumcision|ut nos in gentibus, ipsi autem in circumcisione]] should preach the gospel.

paras.t: Itaque Jacobus iste sanctissimus, Judæorum conversioni ac gubernationi specialiter deputatus, hanc Judæis scripsit epistolam. Et in hoc sua patet profunda humilitas, quod scilicet quum esset latissimæ æstimationis et consanguineus Christi (utpote qui filius erat sororis virginis Mariæ Christiferæ, et primus, ut dictum est, Jerosolymitarum præsul), non tamen Christi apostolum se appellat, sed servum : servum utique, non servitute servilis, sed filialis timoris. Cui servo in Evangelio dicitur : Euge, serve bone et fidelis, etc. Sic quippe et Christus, quem replevit Spiritus timoris Domini, servus Dei secundum assumptam naturam vocatur, juxta illud : In scientia sua justificabit ipse servus meus plurimos, et peccatum eorum portabit. Denique Jacobus opportune vocat se servum Christi, non apostolum, quoniam scripsit Judæis, qui ad superbiam proni erant, et contempserunt gentiles, atque ex gentilitate conversis se præferebant, ut in Actibus Apostolorum et epistolis Pauli, pluribus patet locis. Illos ergo volens suo exemplo ad humilitatem inducere, Christi se nominat servum, potius quam apostolum. Sic et excellentissima atque humillima virgo Maria in suis ad S. Ignatium epistolis, non genitricem seu matrem, sed ancillam Christi se nuncupat. Quibus exemplis percutitur et damnatur superbia nostra. Quia si aliquid sublimitatis competit nobis, hoc […] sumus manifestare directe aut indirecte, explicite sive implicite; quod vero imperfectionis, vitii aut vilitatis nostræ est, subticemus.
paras.en: So this most holy James, specially appointed to the conversion and government of the Jews, wrote this epistle to the Jews. And in this his deep humility is plain: that though he was held in the very highest esteem and was a kinsman of Christ (being the son of the sister of the Virgin Mary, the Mother of Christ, and, as was said, the first bishop of Jerusalem), yet he does not call himself an apostle of Christ but a servant: a servant, that is, not by the servitude of servile fear but of filial fear [that is, the fear of a son, who dreads offending his father, as against the fear of a slave, who dreads punishment]. To such a servant it is said in the Gospel: [[Matt 25:21|Well done, good and faithful servant|Euge, serve bone et fidelis]], etc. So too Christ, whom the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled, is called the servant of God according to the nature He assumed, as in that saying: [[Is 53:11|by his knowledge shall this my just servant justify many, and he shall bear their iniquities|In scientia sua justificabit ipse servus meus plurimos, et peccatum eorum portabit]]. Lastly, James fittingly calls himself the servant of Christ and not an apostle, because he was writing to Jews, who were prone to pride, despised the Gentiles, and set themselves above those converted from the Gentiles, as is plain in many places of the Acts of the Apostles and of Paul's epistles. Wishing, then, to lead them to humility by his example, he names himself the servant of Christ rather than an apostle. So also the most excellent and most humble Virgin Mary, in her letters to St. Ignatius, calls herself not the mother but the handmaid of Christ. By these examples our pride is struck and condemned. For if anything of loftiness belongs to us, this we are […] to make known, directly or indirectly, explicitly or implicitly; but what belongs to our imperfection, vice or baseness we pass over in silence.

paras.t: Porro quod ait, Dei et Domini nostri Jesu Christi, potest exponi dupliciter, scilicet transitive, et intransitive. Potest enim ad eamdem referri personam, ut sit sensus : Jacobus servus Jesu Christi, qui est Deus et Dominus noster : de quo in Joanne legitur, Hic est verus Deus et vita æterna; et alibi, Vocabitur nomen ejus, Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus, Fortis. Potest quoque ad distinctas personas referri, eritque sensus : Jacobus servus Christi Domini nostri, et Dei, id est Patris æterni, cujus Christus est Filius; cujus et Christus in Scripturis vocatur, prout homo, in quantum plenitudine gratiæ unctus est ab eo, juxta illud in Psalmo : Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ. Unde et ait sacratissimus princeps Apostolorum : Jesum unxit Deus Spiritu Sancto et virtute. Et apud Lucam habetur : Responsum accepit Simeon a Spiritu Sancto, non visurum se mortem, nisi prius videret Christum Domini. Et rursus, ubi recitatur Christus interrogasse Apostolos, Quem me dicunt homines esse? Petrus legitur respondisse : Christum Dei. Insuper non solum a Patre unctus est Christus ut homo, sed item a Spiritu Sancto, secundum quod ipsemet protestatur : Spiritus Domini super me, eo quod unxerit me. Imo, quum opera superbenedictæ Trinitatis ad extra sint indivisa, Christus homo a se ipso, prout Deus est, unctus est. Idcirco, dum ipse vocatur Christus Dei, nomine Dei intelligi potest non solum persona Patris, sed et Deus Trinitas, ac quælibet increata Persona : quamvis usitatius et magis proprie dicatur Christus Patris, quam Personæ alterius. — Si exponatur primo modo, tunc per verba ista destruitur hæresis impiissimi Arii, deitatem Christi negantis. Si secundo modo, per ea destruitur perfidia condemnati Sabellii, qui Patris et Filii unam dixit esse personam.
paras.en: Next, the words [[1:1|of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ|Dei et Domini nostri Jesu Christi]] can be expounded in two ways, namely transitively and intransitively [that is, as naming two Persons, God the Father and Christ, or as naming one Person, Christ, who is both God and Lord]. For they can be referred to the same Person, so that the sense is: James, the servant of Jesus Christ, who is our God and Lord; of whom we read in John, [[1 John 5:20|This is the true God and life eternal|Hic est verus Deus et vita æterna]]; and elsewhere, [[Is 9:6|his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God the Mighty|Vocabitur nomen ejus, Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus, Fortis]]. They can also be referred to distinct Persons, and then the sense will be: James, the servant of Christ our Lord, and of God, that is, of the eternal Father, whose Son Christ is; and whose Christ, too, He is called in the Scriptures, as man, inasmuch as He was anointed by Him with the fulness of grace, according to that saying in the Psalm: [[Ps 44:8|God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness|Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ]]. Hence the most holy prince of the Apostles also says of Jesus: [[Acts 10:38|God anointed him with the Holy Ghost and with power|Jesum unxit Deus Spiritu Sancto et virtute]]. And in Luke we have: Simeon had [[Luke 2:26|received an answer from the Holy Ghost, that he should not see death before he had seen the Christ of the Lord|Responsum accepit Simeon a Spiritu Sancto, non visurum se mortem, nisi prius videret Christum Domini]]. And again, where Christ is related to have asked the Apostles, [[Luke 9:18|Whom do the people say that I am|Quem me dicunt homines esse?]]? Peter is read to have answered: [[Luke 9:20|The Christ of God|Christum Dei]]. Moreover, Christ as man was anointed not only by the Father but also by the Holy Ghost, as He Himself declares: [[Is 61:1|The spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord hath anointed me|Spiritus Domini super me, eo quod unxerit me]]. Indeed, since the works of the most blessed Trinity outside itself are undivided, Christ as man was anointed by Himself, inasmuch as He is God. Therefore, when He is called the Christ of God, by the name of God can be understood not only the Person of the Father but also God the Trinity, and any uncreated Person; although He is more usually and more properly called the Christ of the Father than of another Person. — If the words are expounded in the first way, they destroy the heresy of the most impious Arius, who denied the Godhead of Christ. If in the second way, they destroy the false teaching of the condemned Sabellius, who said that the Father and the Son are one person.

paras.t: Itaque, Jacobus Christi servus, non servitute (ut tactum est) servilis timoris : de cujusmodi servo ait Salvator, Servus non manet in domo in æternum. Hic Jacobus scribit ac mandat, imprecatur et optat duodecim tribubus quæ sunt in dispersione, salutem. Ante Babylonicam captivitatem, captæ erant decem tribus Israel ab Assyriis, nec interim sunt reductæ. Post captivitatem autem Babylonicam, tribus Juda ac Benjamin redierunt in propria, et cum eis tribus Levitica, ut patet in Esdra. Quomodo ergo Jacobus scribere potuit duodecim tribubus Israel dispersis, quum aliquæ earum essent reductæ? Certumque est quod non scripsit decem tribubus remote a Judæa translatis, incredulis, et ultra montes Caspios constitutis. Et respondendum, quod ex decem tribubus aliqui remanserunt in Judæa, et crediderunt in Christum. Similiter ex tribu Juda et Levi ac Benjamin multa millia fuerunt ad Christum conversa, ut patet in Actibus : ubi et Lucas evangelista testatur, quod etiam multa sacerdotum turba obediebat fidei; et quod erant in Jerusalem habitantes Judæi, viri religiosi, ex omni natione quæ sub cœlo est. Ex quibus plurimi sunt conversi : qui et paulo post, Stephano protomartyre lapidato, sunt ab obstinatis incredulisque Judæis ab Jerusalem pulsi, et per regiones Judææ atque Samariæ, et per alia loca diversa dispersi. Ex qua dispersione non minorata, sed aucta fuit evangelica fides, quia dispersi undique prædicabant. Hinc in Actibus habetur : Facta est autem in illa die persecutio magna in Ecclesia quæ erat Jerosolymis, et omnes dispersi sunt per regiones Judææ et Samariæ, præter Apostolos; et qui dispersi erant, pertransibant evangelizantes verbum Dei.
paras.en: So James, the servant of Christ, not (as was touched on) by the servitude of servile fear: of such a servant the Saviour says, [[John 8:35|the servant abideth not in the house for ever|Servus non manet in domo in æternum]]. This James writes and sends, invokes and wishes [[1:1|to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad, greeting|duodecim tribubus quæ sunt in dispersione, salutem]]. Before the Babylonian captivity the ten tribes of Israel had been taken captive by the Assyrians[[4 Kings 17:6||]], and they were not brought back in the meantime. But after the Babylonian captivity the tribes of Juda and Benjamin returned to their own land, and with them the tribe of Levi, as is plain in Esdras[[1 Esd 1:5||]]. How, then, could James write to the twelve tribes of Israel as scattered, when some of them had been brought back? And it is certain that he did not write to the ten tribes carried far away from Judea, unbelieving, and settled beyond the Caspian mountains. The answer is that of the ten tribes some remained in Judea and believed in Christ. Likewise of the tribes of Juda, Levi and Benjamin many thousands were converted to Christ, as is plain in the Acts[[Acts 2:41||]][[Acts 4:4||]][[Acts 5:14||]], where Luke the Evangelist also testifies that [[Acts 6:7|A great multitude also of the priests obeyed the faith|multa sacerdotum turba obediebat fidei]]; and that [[Acts 2:5|there were dwelling at Jerusalem, Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven|erant in Jerusalem habitantes Judæi, viri religiosi, ex omni natione quæ sub cœlo est]]. Of these very many were converted; and shortly afterwards, when Stephen the protomartyr had been stoned, they were driven from Jerusalem by the obstinate and unbelieving Jews and scattered through the countries of Judea and Samaria and through various other places. By this dispersion the faith of the Gospel was not lessened but increased, for those who were scattered preached everywhere. Hence we have in the Acts: [[Acts 8:1|there was raised a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem. And they were all dispersed through the countries of Judea, and Samaria, except the apostles|Facta est autem in illa die persecutio magna in Ecclesia quæ erat Jerosolymis, et omnes dispersi sunt per regiones Judææ et Samariæ, præter Apostolos]]; and [[Acts 8:4|They therefore that were dispersed went about preaching the word of God|qui dispersi erant, pertransibant evangelizantes verbum Dei]].

paras.t: Ex præinductis constat, ineptam esse expositionem dicentis, quod Jacobus scripsit dispersis extra terminum Judææ, ita ut eis non scripserit qui intra Judæam erant dispersi, eo quod illos potuit verbo docere. Imo dicendum, quod non potuit illos verbo docere, qui per tam diversas urbes, regiones et distantias dispersi fuerunt. Nec Jacobus iste legitur passim extra Jerusalem ivisse ad prædicandum. Nec sequitur : Potuit eos verbo informare, ergo non docuit eos scripto : quoniam etsi informatio per verba vocalia efficacior sit quam per verba scripta, tamen instructio per scripta perseverantior perhibetur, atque ad posteriorum quoque magis manet memoriam. Unde Paulus apostolus multos instruxit per epistolas, quos et ante et postea docuit verbis. Joannes quoque apostolus ab exsilio Patmos reversus, scripsit Evangelium iis quos et quotidianis instruxit sermonibus. Sic et Lucas in exordio Actuum Apostolorum, insinuat se ei Actus Apostolorum Evangeliumque scripsisse, puta Theophilo, quem et verbis edocuit. Insuper Marcus scripsit Evangelium suum Romæ, rogatus a fidelibus ibi, qui non solum a Marco, sed etiam a principe Apostolorum Petro quotidie edocebantur vocaliter. Matthæus etiam Nubianos verbo instruxit ac scripto.
paras.en: From what has been brought forward it is clear that the exposition is unsound which says that James wrote to those scattered outside the bounds of Judea, so that he did not write to those scattered within Judea, because he could teach them by word of mouth. Rather we must say that he could not teach by word of mouth those who were scattered through so many different cities, countries and distances. Nor do we read that this James went about here and there outside Jerusalem to preach. Nor does it follow, "He could instruct them by word of mouth, therefore he did not teach them in writing": for although instruction by spoken words is more effective than by written ones, instruction by writing is held to be more lasting, and it remains better in the memory of those who come after. Hence Paul the Apostle instructed many by his epistles whom he taught by word both before and afterwards. John the Apostle too, on returning from his exile in Patmos, wrote the Gospel for those whom he also instructed with daily discourses. So also Luke, at the beginning of the Acts of the Apostles, gives us to understand that he wrote the Acts of the Apostles and the Gospel for one whom he had also taught by word, namely Theophilus[[Acts 1:1||]]. Moreover, Mark wrote his Gospel at Rome, at the request of the faithful there, who were taught daily by word of mouth not only by Mark but also by Peter, the prince of the Apostles. Matthew also instructed the Nubians by word and by writing.

paras.t: Itaque, dispersis tribubus mandavit Jacobus iste salutem, videlicet beatitudinem viæ ac patriæ, hoc est meritum et profectum gratiæ ac virtutum, et gloriam patriæ. Et quia in dispersione et tribulatione fuerunt, informationem eorum a patientia incipit. Dispersi namque et afflicti, tali instructione consolationeque indigent. Omne gaudium existimate, fratres mei, quum in tentationes varias incideritis. Ecce quam caritativa et sapientialis consolatio, quam dulcis et pia, quam compendiosa efficaxque instructio! Spirituales filios suos ac subditos vocat humiliter fratres suos. Per quod quorumdam, in oculis suis magnorum, animositas reprobatur, qui subditos suos, aut inferiores, aut certe æquales, nesciunt quasi fratres apprehendere, et humili appellatione exprimere, illud Ecclesiastici non advertentes : Rectorem te posuerunt? noli extolli; esto in illis quasi unus ex eis; curam illorum habe, et sic considera. Hinc in Deuteronomio Deus præcepit de rege : Non elevetur cor ejus in superbiam super fratres suos. Si igitur regibus et prælatis tam prohibitum est atque damnabile, se super subditos suos extollere, quanto est iniquius damnabiliusque, si quis se elevet super eos quibus non præest, aut super æquales, et potissimum super majores superioresque suos? Quod prorsus diabolicum est.
paras.en: So to the scattered tribes this James sent [[1:1|greeting|salutem]] [the Latin *salus* means both "greeting" (health, welfare) and "salvation"], that is, the blessedness of the way and of the fatherland: the merit and progress of grace and the virtues, and the glory of the fatherland [that is, of this life, the road to heaven, and of heaven itself]. And because they were in dispersion and tribulation, he begins his instruction of them with patience. For the scattered and afflicted need such instruction and consolation. [[1:2|My brethren, count it all joy, when you shall fall into divers temptations|Omne gaudium existimate, fratres mei, quum in tentationes varias incideritis]]. See how loving and wise a consolation, how sweet and holy, how brief and effective an instruction! He humbly calls his spiritual sons and subjects his brethren. By this is rebuked the arrogance of some who are great in their own eyes, who do not know how to regard their subjects, or their inferiors, or even their equals, as brethren, and to address them with a humble name, not heeding that saying of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 32:1|Have they made thee ruler? be not lifted up: be among them as one of them|Rectorem te posuerunt? noli extolli; esto in illis quasi unus ex eis]]; [[Ecclus 32:2|Have care of them, and so sit down|curam illorum habe, et sic considera]] [Denis reads *considera*, "consider", where the Vulgate has *conside*, "sit down"]. Hence in Deuteronomy God commanded of the king: [[Deut 17:20|that his heart be not lifted up with pride over his brethren|Non elevetur cor ejus in superbiam super fratres suos]]. If, then, it is so forbidden and damnable for kings and prelates to exalt themselves over their subjects, how much more wicked and damnable is it if someone raises himself above those over whom he has no charge, or above his equals, and above all above his elders and superiors? This is altogether devilish.

paras.t: Itaque, fratres mei : fratres utique conformitate naturæ specificæ, ac identitate originalis propagationis humanæ; fratres quoque fide et religione, et quia ejusdem Patris cœlestis filii adoptivi, atque ad eamdem hereditatem supernam vocati. Propter quod quotidie dicimus : Pater noster qui es in cœlis, adveniat regnum tuum, hoc est, ad cœlestis regni participationem nos provehe, ut ædificentur ex nobis muri cœlestis ac triumphantis Jerusalem, et regnum impleatur cœleste. Fraterne ergo nos invicem diligamus, nec unus alium aspernetur. Scriptum enim est : Numquid non pater unus omnium nostrum? Numquid non Deus unus creavit nos? Quare ergo despicit unusquisque fratrem suum?
paras.en: So, [[1:2|My brethren|fratres mei]]: brethren, that is, by sharing the same specific nature [that is, the nature of the human species], and by the sameness of our original descent as men; brethren also by faith and religion, and because we are adopted sons of the same heavenly Father, and called to the same inheritance on high. For this reason we say daily: [[Matt 6:9|Our Father who art in heaven|Pater noster qui es in cœlis]], [[Matt 6:10|Thy kingdom come|adveniat regnum tuum]]: that is, bring us to a share in the heavenly kingdom, so that from us the walls of the heavenly and triumphant Jerusalem may be built up[[Ps 50:20||]] [the margin gives Ps. i, 20; the words are from Ps 50:20, "that the walls of Jerusalem may be built up"], and the heavenly kingdom be filled. Let us therefore love one another as brothers, and let no one despise another. For it is written: [[Mal 2:10|Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us? why then doth every one of us despise his brother|Numquid non pater unus omnium nostrum? Numquid non Deus unus creavit nos? Quare ergo despicit unusquisque fratrem suum?]]?

paras.t: Sic ergo, o fratres, omne gaudium existimate, id est, perfectam jucunditatem judicate consistere in hoc, quum in diversas tentationes incideritis, id est, in multas et magnas tribulationes et adversitates veneritis. Quoniam, quamvis tribulatio in se ipsa amara sit et pœnalis, tamen multipliciter utilis est, et fructuosa quam maxime; idcirco cum gaudio spirituali est acceptanda et sustinenda. Si enim Dei intuitu et amore æquanimiter toleretur, purgat a vitiis, disponit ad gratiam eamque auget, et virtutes augmentat, et Christo propter nos passo patientem conformat. Est quoque signum probabile prædestinationis æternæ, et filiationis adoptivæ, ac dilectionis Dei ad hominem, Deo testante : Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo. Sed et per eam a futuris eripimur pœnis, et ad beatitudinem pleniorem compendiosius pervenimus. Quum ergo fructuosissimum ac saluberrimum sit, in præsenti paterne castigari, multipliciter tribulari, adversitatibus exerceri, corripi et tentari, dummodo patienter feratur : nonne insipientiæ et magnæ imperfectionis, imo insaniæ est indicium, quod nolumus adversitates, correptiones, tentationes, correctiones libenter sufferre, sed statim irascimur, indignamur, turbamur, dejicimur, imo vix pro peccatis et excessibus nostris corripi ac corrigi volumus? quum tamen princeps Apostolorum dicat : Hæc est gratia, si propter conscientiam Dei sustinet quis tristitias, patiens injuste. Quæ enim est gratia, si peccantes et colaphizati suffertis? Si autem benefacientes sustinetis, hæc est gratia apud Deum : in hoc enim vocati estis. Hæc est christianæ sapientiæ altitudo, hæc Christi doctrina, in adversis sicut in omnibus divitiis gloriari, sicque Salvatoris sectari vestigia, qui ait : Beati estis quum maledixerint vobis homines, et persecuti vos fuerint, et dixerint omne malum adversum vos, mentientes, propter me; gaudete in illa hora et exsultate, quoniam merces vestra copiosa est in cœlis.
paras.en: So then, O brethren, [[1:2|count it all joy|omne gaudium existimate]], that is, judge that perfect gladness lies in this, [[1:2|when you shall fall into divers temptations|quum in diversas tentationes incideritis]], that is, when you come into many and great tribulations and adversities. For although tribulation in itself is bitter and painful, yet it is useful in many ways and fruitful in the highest degree; therefore it is to be accepted and borne with spiritual joy. For if it is borne with an even mind, with regard to God and for love of Him, it cleanses from vices, disposes to grace and increases it, augments the virtues, and conforms the sufferer to Christ, who suffered for us[[1 Pet 4:1||]]. It is also a probable sign of eternal predestination, of adoptive sonship, and of God's love for man, as God testifies: [[Apoc 3:19|Such as I love, I rebuke and chastise|Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo]]. And through it we are also delivered from punishments to come, and reach a fuller blessedness by a shorter way. Since, then, it is most fruitful and most wholesome to be chastised as by a father in this present life, to be troubled in many ways, exercised by adversities, rebuked and tried, provided it is borne patiently: is it not a sign of folly and of great imperfection, nay of madness, that we will not willingly bear adversities, rebukes, temptations and corrections, but at once grow angry, indignant, troubled and downcast, and are scarcely willing to be rebuked and corrected even for our sins and excesses? And this though the prince of the Apostles says: [[1 Pet 2:19|this is thankworthy: if, for conscience towards God, a man endure sorrows, suffering wrongfully|Hæc est gratia, si propter conscientiam Dei sustinet quis tristitias, patiens injuste]] [*gratia*, here "thankworthy", is literally "grace" or "favour"]. [[1 Pet 2:20|For what glory is it, if, committing sin and being buffeted for it, you endure? But if doing well you suffer patiently: this is thankworthy before God|Quæ enim est gratia, si peccantes et colaphizati suffertis? Si autem benefacientes sustinetis, hæc est gratia apud Deum]] [Denis reads *gratia* here too, where the Vulgate has *gloria*, "glory"]: [[1 Pet 2:21|For unto this are you called|in hoc enim vocati estis]]. This is the height of Christian wisdom, this the teaching of Christ: to glory in adversities as in all riches, and so to follow in the footsteps of the Saviour, who says: [[Matt 5:11|Blessed are ye when they shall revile you, and persecute you, and speak all that is evil against you, untruly, for my sake|Beati estis quum maledixerint vobis homines, et persecuti vos fuerint, et dixerint omne malum adversum vos, mentientes, propter me]]; [[Matt 5:12|Be glad and rejoice for your reward is very great in heaven|gaudete in illa hora et exsultate, quoniam merces vestra copiosa est in cœlis]][[Luke 6:22||]][[Luke 6:23||]] [Denis's wording is Matthew's, with *homines*, "men", and *in illa hora*, "in that hour", recalling Luke's "men" and "in that day"].

paras.t: Sic igitur omne gaudium existimate, id est, omni gaudio dignum arbitramini, diversas tentationes incidere, et eas æquanimiter sustinere : quia per hoc spiritualem consolationem in via, et plenam felicitatem in patria promeretur ac obtinet homo; imo, teste Apostolo, non sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam. Etenim futuræ mercedis ac gloriæ comparatione, omnis tribulatio in hac vita est modicissima reputanda, juxta illud : Id quod in præsenti est momentaneum et leve tribulationis nostræ, supra modum in sublimitate æternum gloriæ pondus operatur in nobis. Quum ergo infirmi patiantur se uri, secari, incidi pro transitoria sanitate, quid est quod adversa perpeti dedignamur pro æterna salute? Recte itaque disseruit Salomon : Qui impatiens est, operatur stultitiam. Denique in tribulationibus maxime pronus est Deus misereri et parcere, quemadmodum ait : Cum ipso sum in tribulatione, eripiam eum, et glorificabo eum.
paras.en: So, then, [[1:2|count it all joy|omne gaudium existimate]], that is, think it worthy of all joy to fall into divers temptations and to bear them with an even mind: for by this a man merits and obtains spiritual consolation on the way and full happiness in the fatherland; indeed, as the Apostle witnesses, [[Rom 8:18|the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come|non sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam]]. For in comparison with the reward and glory to come, every tribulation in this life is to be reckoned very slight, according to that saying: [[2 Cor 4:17|that which is at present momentary and light of our tribulation worketh for us above measure, exceedingly an eternal weight of glory|Id quod in præsenti est momentaneum et leve tribulationis nostræ, supra modum in sublimitate æternum gloriæ pondus operatur in nobis]]. Since, then, the sick allow themselves to be burned, cut and lanced for a passing health, why is it that we disdain to suffer adversities for eternal salvation? Rightly, therefore, did Solomon declare: [[Prov 14:17|The impatient man shall work folly|Qui impatiens est, operatur stultitiam]]. Lastly, in tribulations God is most inclined to have mercy and to spare, as He says: [[Ps 90:15|I am with him in tribulation, I will deliver him, and I will glorify him|Cum ipso sum in tribulatione, eripiam eum, et glorificabo eum]].

paras.t: Deinde subjungitur ratio cur tentationes seu tribulationes pro Deo, pro fide, pro justitia, sint cum gaudio perferenda. Scientes quod probatio fidei vestræ, id est ipsa vestri persecutio, tribulatio, sive tentatio pro causis prætactis : per quam fides vestra probatur, examinatur et exercetur, ut pateat an vere et firmiter insit vobis; et vos ipsi probamini, an vere in fide sitis constantes, et Deo fideliter adhærentes : quod probatur, inquiritur, et declaratur per hoc quod nec propter adversa fidem ejus relinquitis, neque ab eo vos separatis. Hinc scriptum est : Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit electos Deus. Dicitur autem Deus electos et fidem eorum probare et examinare per adversa, non ut ei innotescant, sed ut electi cognoscant se ipsos, eorumque virtus et fides aliis ad eorum ædificationem et Dei honorem patescant. Propter quod loquitur : Ducam eos per ignem, et uram eos sicut uritur argentum, et probabo eos sicut probatur aurum. Porro per tribulationem æquanimiter toleratam, fides et virtus hominis probantur, hoc est, a summo Judice approbantur, atque hominibus demonstrantur, ut eas sectentur. Sic ergo probatio fidei vestræ, patientiam operatur, id est, ad habitualem et firmam patientiam vos inducit : quia ex actibus sæpe reiteratis habitus generatur : et ex frequentibus patientiis in adversis, seu patientibus adversitatum tolerationibus frequentatis, generatur in homine patientiæ virtus, seu patientia firma et habitualis, per quam homo facile ac hilariter patitur, quod ante cum difficultate et renisione patiebatur.
paras.en: Next is added the reason why temptations or tribulations for God, for the faith, for justice, are to be borne with joy. [[1:3|Knowing that the trying of your faith|Scientes quod probatio fidei vestræ]], that is, your very persecution, tribulation or temptation for the causes already touched on: by which your faith is tried, examined and exercised, so that it may be seen whether it is truly and firmly in you; and you yourselves are tried, whether you are truly constant in the faith and faithfully cleaving to God: which is tested, searched out and made plain by this, that you neither abandon faith in Him because of adversities nor separate yourselves from Him. Hence it is written: [[Wis 3:6|As gold in the furnace, he hath proved them|Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit electos Deus]] [Denis has "God hath proved the elect" for "he hath proved them"]. Now God is said to try and examine the elect and their faith by adversities, not that they may become known to Him, but that the elect may know themselves, and that their virtue and faith may be shown to others for their edification and the honour of God. For this reason He says: [[Zach 13:9|I will bring the third part through the fire|Ducam eos per ignem]] [Denis has *eos*, "them", for "the third part"], [[Zach 13:9|and will refine them as silver is refined: and I will try them as gold is tried|et uram eos sicut uritur argentum, et probabo eos sicut probatur aurum]]. Further, by tribulation borne with an even mind a man's faith and virtue are proved, that is, approved by the supreme Judge and shown to men, that they may follow them. So, then, [[1:3|the trying of your faith worketh patience|probatio fidei vestræ, patientiam operatur]], that is, leads you to a habitual and firm patience: for a habit is generated from acts often repeated; and from frequent acts of patience in adversities, that is, from patient endurings of adversity often repeated, there is generated in a man the virtue of patience, a firm and habitual patience, by which a man suffers easily and cheerfully what before he suffered with difficulty and resistance.

paras.t: Quocirca sciendum, quod duplex est patientia, puta infusa, et acquisita. Et eadem distinctio in aliis virtutibus assignatur. Estque quæstio non minima, an virtus infusa et acquisita circa idem objectum versantes, specifice distinguantur. Patientia autem infusa inest omni homini in caritate et gratia existenti; sed patientia ista non statim in principio sui aufert ab homine difficultatem sustinendi adversa : quia virtutes infusæ non statim tollunt reliquias vitiorum præteritorum, nisi forsan in magna abundantia et excellentia infundantur. Patientia vero acquisita, tollit difficultatem sufferendi adversa : quia virtutes acquisitæ, vitiorum tollunt reliquias. Unde hujusmodi virtus a Tullio definitur, quod sit habitus rationi consentaneus, in modum naturæ operans. Atque ut ait Philosophus, signum hujusmodi virtutis est delectatio fiens in opere, id est delectatio operationi suæ annexa. Verumtamen virtutes infusæ, etiam paulatim crescunt et perficiuntur : et tunc excellentius tollunt reliquias vitiorum, videlicet pronitatem ad malum, inclinationem ad culpam, et debilitatem resistendi peccatis, quam virtutes acquisitæ. Gratia namque fortior est quam natura. Tunc quoque majorem delectationem sibi annexam habet virtus infusa, quam acquisita.
paras.en: On this point it should be known that patience is twofold, namely infused and acquired [that is, given by God with grace, or gained by one's own repeated acts]. And the same distinction is made in the other virtues. And it is no small question whether an infused and an acquired virtue concerned with the same object differ in species. Now infused patience is in every man who is in charity and grace; but this patience does not at once, at its beginning, take from a man the difficulty of bearing adversities: for infused virtues do not at once remove the remnants of past vices, unless perhaps they are infused in great abundance and excellence. Acquired patience, on the other hand, takes away the difficulty of bearing adversities: for acquired virtues remove the remnants of vices. Hence virtue of this kind is defined by Tully [that is, Cicero] as a habit in agreement with reason, working after the manner of nature. And as the Philosopher [Aristotle] says, the sign of such a virtue is the delight that arises in the deed, that is, the delight joined to its activity. Yet the infused virtues also grow little by little and are perfected; and then they remove the remnants of vices, that is, the proneness to evil, the inclination to sin and the weakness in resisting sins, more excellently than the acquired virtues. For grace is stronger than nature. Then, too, the infused virtue has a greater delight joined to it than the acquired.

paras.t: Sed præinducto verbo apostoli Jacobi asserentis quod probatio patientiam operatur, contrarium videtur quod ad Romanos habetur, ubi dicitur : Tribulatio patientiam operatur, patientia autem probationem, probatio vero spem. Si ergo patientia operatur probationem, quomodo probatio operatur patientiam? Sequeretur enim, quod esset circulatio in causis et causatis, et idem esset causa sui ipsius : quoniam quod est causa causæ, est causa causati. Et respondendum, quod in causis et causatis non est circulatio in eodem genere causæ, sed unum potest esse causa alterius, et ediverso, in diverso genere causæ : quemadmodum ambulatio est causa sanitatis in genere causæ efficientis, sanitas vero causa est ambulationis in genere causæ finalis. Sic in proposito, patientia operatur probationem efficienter; probatio autem formaliter sumpta, operatur patientiam in genere causæ finalis, quia patientia ordinatur ad fidei probationem. Hinc ait Beda : Ideo homo tentatur adversis, ut patientiam discat, et per eam ostendere possit atque probare quod firmam fidem futuræ retributionis gestit in corde. Patientia autem operatur probationem : quia cujus patientia vincit non potest, ille perfectus esse probatur. Unde hoc loco subjungitur : Patientia autem opus perfectum habet. Porro probatio fidei patientiam operatur, quia hac ratione fideles per patientiam exercentur, ut per eam fides eorum, quam sit perfecta, probetur.
paras.en: But against the words of the Apostle James just brought forward, which assert that [[1:3|the trying|probatio]] [[1:3|worketh patience|patientiam operatur]], what we have in Romans seems contrary, where it is said: [[Rom 5:3|tribulation worketh patience|Tribulatio patientiam operatur]]; [[Rom 5:4|And patience trial; and trial hope|patientia autem probationem, probatio vero spem]] [Denis's word is the same *probatio* throughout, which the Douay-Rheims renders "trying" in St. James and "trial" here]. If, then, patience works trial, how does trial work patience? For it would follow that there was a circle in causes and things caused, and that the same thing was the cause of itself: since what is the cause of a cause is the cause of what is caused. The answer is that in causes and things caused there is no circle in the same kind of cause, but one thing can be the cause of another, and the other way about, in different kinds of cause: as walking is the cause of health in the kind of efficient cause, and health is the cause of walking in the kind of final cause [that is, health is that for the sake of which one walks]. So in the case before us, patience works trial as its efficient cause; but trial, taken formally, works patience in the kind of final cause, because patience is ordered to the proving of faith. Hence Bede says: A man is tempted by adversities so that he may learn patience, and through it may be able to show and prove that he bears in his heart a firm faith in the reward to come. And patience works trial: for he whose patience cannot be overcome is proved to be perfect. Hence in this place is added: [[1:4|And patience hath a perfect work|Patientia autem opus perfectum habet]]. Further, the trying of faith works patience, because the faithful are exercised in patience for this reason, that through it it may be proved how perfect their faith is.

paras.t: Sed quum multæ sint virtutes patientia digniores et perfectiores, videlicet virtutes theologicæ, justitia quoque et fortitudo, latria atque prudentia : cur dicitur opus perfectum habere? Respondetur, quod multiplici ratione patientia dicitur opus habere perfectum. Prima et potissima ratio est, quia per integram et constantem patientiam in adversis, præcipue declaratur exstirpatio privati amoris, et aliarum virtutum firmiter radicata sinceritas. Quod enim homo propter adversa impatiens redditur et tristatur, hinc accidit quoniam amat se in se, et nondum spiritualiter mortuus est sibimetipsi, seu propriæ voluntati et naturali inclinationi, sed adhuc amat honores et commoda sua. Similiter si homo sit veraciter humilis, mitis, timoratus et fractus, per patientiam maxime declaratur et investigatur. Nempe, si quis sit ficte seu apparenter mitis, humilis, fractus, et in camino adversitatis ponatur, seu tribulationibus exerceatur; protinus interiorem suam imperfectionem ostendit, et per impatientiæ suæ impetum ebullit, suamque elationem, iram, infractionem demonstrat : quemadmodum si mala olla ponatur in igne, mox crepit et exsilit. Qui vero invincibiliter patiens invenitur, a præfatis vitiis immunis probatur, et vere virtuosus esse cognoscitur, vivens Deo, non sibi ipsi.
paras.en: But since there are many virtues worthier and more perfect than patience, namely the theological virtues, and also justice and fortitude, latria [that is, the worship due to God alone] and prudence, why is patience said to have a perfect work? The answer is that patience is said to have a perfect work for many reasons. The first and chief reason is that by an entire and constant patience in adversities the rooting out of private love [that is, self-love] and the firmly rooted sincerity of the other virtues are above all made plain. For that a man is made impatient and sad by adversities comes about because he loves himself in himself, and has not yet died spiritually to himself, that is, to his own will and natural inclination, but still loves his own honours and comforts. Likewise, whether a man is truly humble, meek, God-fearing and broken [that is, contrite, his self-will crushed] is shown and searched out above all by patience. For if anyone is meek, humble and broken only in pretence or appearance, and is put in the furnace of adversity or exercised by tribulations, he at once shows his inner imperfection, boils over in the rush of his impatience, and displays his pride, his anger, his unbrokenness: just as a bad pot put on the fire soon cracks and flies apart. But he who is found unconquerably patient is proved to be free of the said vices, and is known to be truly virtuous, living to God, not to himself[[2 Cor 5:15||]].

paras.t: Secunda ratio hujus est, quia (ut scribit hoc loco Albertus Magnus) patientia habet opera sex, suo modo perfecta. Primum est, probatio hominis ac virtutum ipsius : quia, ut dictum est, patientia operatur probationem. Hinc religiosi a superioribus suis et a se invicem per quædam adversa exerceri consueverunt, ut quales sint comprobentur ac manifestentur. Secundum est, quo[…]dium spirituale, exspectatioque lætitiæ. Propter quod in Ecclesiastico scriptum est : Usque ad tempus sustinebit patiens, et postea erit ei redditio jucunditatis. Et Apostolus quoque : Gloriamur, inquit, in tribulationibus. Per patientiam namque meretur homo, etiam in præsenti, divinitus consolari, quemadmodum Paulus fatetur : Benedictus Deus qui consolatur nos in omni tribulatione nostra. Et iterum, Sicut abundant passiones Christi in nobis, ita per Christum abundat consolatio nostra. Hoc est quod ait Psalmista : Secundum multitudinem dolorum meorum in corde meo, consolationes tuæ lætificaverunt animam meam. Sed hanc consolationem quidam per impatientiam et murmurationem suam auferunt sibi. Idcirco in Job scribitur : Numquid grande est ut consoleretur te Deus? Sed verba tua prava hoc prohibent. Tertium opus est, iræ ac rancoris exstinctio, juxta illud Sapientis : Vir iracundus provocat rixas; qui autem patiens est, mitigat suscitatas. Quartum est, passionum subjectio et sui ipsius salubris possessio. Propter quod ait Salvator : In patientia vestra possidebitis animas vestras. Impatiens quippe, se ipsum non possidet, sed a sua impatientia, ira, tristitia, turbulentia possidetur. Patiens autem se possidet, quoniam inferiores vires et passiones subjicit rationi. Quintum est, sui ipsius gubernatio circumspecta. Unde in Proverbiis : Qui patiens est, multa gubernatur prudentia; qui autem impatiens est, exaltat stultitiam suam. Sextum est, vitæ æternæ adeptio, prout ad Hebræos legitur : Patientia vobis necessaria est, ut voluntatem Dei facientes, reportetis promissionem. Hinc Scriptura patientiam valde commendat. Et patientiam semper amplecti et observare debemus, quum Salomon dicat : Melior est patiens viro forti; et qui dominatur animo suo, expugnatore urbium.
paras.en: The second reason for this is that (as Albert the Great writes on this place) patience has six works, each perfect in its own way. The first is the proving of a man and of his virtues: for, as was said, patience works trial. Hence religious are accustomed to be exercised by their superiors and by one another with certain adversities, so that it may be proved and made plain what they are. The second is that by which […]…dium spirituale [the text is lost here; the broken word is probably *gaudium*, so "spiritual joy"], and the expectation of gladness. For this reason it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 1:29|A patient man shall bear for a time, and afterwards joy shall be restored to him|Usque ad tempus sustinebit patiens, et postea erit ei redditio jucunditatis]]. And the Apostle too: [[Rom 5:3|we glory|Gloriamur]], he says, [[Rom 5:3|in tribulation|in tribulationibus]]. For by patience a man merits to be consoled by God even in this present life, as Paul declares: [[2 Cor 1:3|Blessed be the God|Benedictus Deus]] [[2 Cor 1:4|Who comforteth us in all our tribulation|qui consolatur nos in omni tribulatione nostra]]. And again: [[2 Cor 1:5|as the sufferings of Christ abound in us: so also by Christ doth our comfort abound|Sicut abundant passiones Christi in nobis, ita per Christum abundat consolatio nostra]]. This is what the Psalmist says: [[Ps 93:19|According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, thy comforts have given joy to my soul.|Secundum multitudinem dolorum meorum in corde meo, consolationes tuæ lætificaverunt animam meam]]. But some take this consolation away from themselves by their impatience and murmuring. Therefore it is written in Job: [[Job 15:11|Is it a great matter that God should comfort thee? but thy wicked words hinder this|Numquid grande est ut consoleretur te Deus? Sed verba tua prava hoc prohibent]]. The third work is the quenching of anger and rancour, according to that saying of the Wise Man: [[Prov 15:18|A passionate man stirreth up strifes: he that is patient appeaseth those that are stirred up|Vir iracundus provocat rixas; qui autem patiens est, mitigat suscitatas]]. The fourth is the subjection of the passions and the wholesome possession of oneself. For this reason the Saviour says: [[Luke 21:19|In your patience you shall possess your souls.|In patientia vestra possidebitis animas vestras]]. For the impatient man does not possess himself, but is possessed by his impatience, anger, sadness and turmoil. But the patient man possesses himself, since he subjects his lower powers and passions to reason. The fifth is a circumspect government of oneself. Hence in Proverbs: [[Prov 14:29|He that is patient, is governed with much wisdom: but he that is impatient, exalteth his folly|Qui patiens est, multa gubernatur prudentia; qui autem impatiens est, exaltat stultitiam suam]]. The sixth is the attainment of eternal life, as we read in Hebrews: [[Heb 10:36|patience is necessary for you: that, doing the will of God, you may receive the promise|Patientia vobis necessaria est, ut voluntatem Dei facientes, reportetis promissionem]]. Hence Scripture commends patience highly. And we ought always to embrace and keep patience, since Solomon says: [[Prov 16:32|The patient man is better than the valiant: and he that ruleth his spirit, than he that taketh cities|Melior est patiens viro forti; et qui dominatur animo suo, expugnatore urbium]].

paras.t: Tertia ratio hujus est, quoniam patientia refrenat tristitiam : qua refrenata, refrenantur et ira ac odium. Patientia namque circa passionem tristitiæ refrenandam versatur. In tribulationibus autem et persecutionibus, passio quæ prima occurrit sustinenti, est tristitia : ex qua protinus nascitur ira, quæ est appetitus ultionis de persequente, injuriam irrogante, seu offendente; deinde oritur odium. Qui igitur per patientiam refrenat tristitiam, amputat iram ac odium. Unde qui de tribulatione sibi inflicta non contristatur, contra tribulantem nequaquam irascitur, nec odit eumdem.
paras.en: The third reason for this is that patience bridles sadness; and when sadness is bridled, anger and hatred are bridled too. For patience is concerned with bridling the passion of sadness. Now in tribulations and persecutions the passion that first meets the sufferer is sadness: from it anger at once springs, which is the desire of vengeance on the one who persecutes, does wrong or offends; then hatred arises. He, then, who bridles sadness by patience cuts off anger and hatred. Hence he who is not saddened by the tribulation inflicted on him is in no way angry with the one who troubles him, nor does he hate him.

paras.t: Sicque quantum ad hæc, patientia habet opus perfectum. Ideo subditur : Ut sitis perfecti in omni virtute, et integri in recta intentione, et tota mente Deo adhærere ac complacere intendatis atque conemini; et ita cum Propheta cantare possitis, Confitebor tibi, Domine, in toto corde meo, utputa intellectu et affectu, ratione et voluntate, actu et intentione. Ista est spiritualis interiorque integritas, qua quis tota mente Deo intentus est : non partim Deo et partim mundo, ut hi qui Deo et mundo cupiunt deservire ac complacere : contra quos loquitur Christus, Nemo potest duobus dominis servire; et rursus, Non potestis Deo servire et mammonæ. De quibus Propheta : Divisum est cor eorum, nunc interibunt. Sit ergo semper tota nostra intentio et omnis affectio ad Deum, et in Deo, videlicet reducta, simplificata, fixa et adunata in eo. In nullo deficientes ab exsecutione operum bonorum, nec tentationibus succumbentes, sed perseverantes usque in finem, quemadmodum monet Apostolus : In omnibus semper omnem sufficientiam habentes, abundetis in omne opus bonum.
paras.en: And so, as regards these things, [[1:4|patience hath a perfect work|patientia habet opus perfectum]]. Therefore is added: [[1:4|that you may be perfect|Ut sitis perfecti]] in every virtue, [[1:4|and entire|et integri]] in right intention, and may aim and strive with your whole mind to cleave to God and please Him; and so may be able to sing with the Prophet, [[Ps 9:2|I will give praise to thee, O Lord, with my whole heart|Confitebor tibi, Domine, in toto corde meo]], that is, with understanding and affection, reason and will, deed and intention. This is the spiritual and inner entireness by which one is intent on God with one's whole mind: not partly on God and partly on the world, like those who desire to serve and please both God and the world; against whom Christ speaks, [[Matt 6:24|No man can serve two masters|Nemo potest duobus dominis servire]]; and again, [[Matt 6:24|You cannot serve God and mammon|Non potestis Deo servire et mammonæ]]. Of them the Prophet says: [[Osee 10:2|Their heart is divided: now they shall perish|Divisum est cor eorum, nunc interibunt]]. Let all our intention, then, and all our affection be always towards God and in God, that is, led back, made simple, fixed and made one in Him. [[1:4|failing in nothing|In nullo deficientes]] in carrying out good works, not yielding to temptations, but persevering to the end, as the Apostle admonishes: [[2 Cor 9:8|always, having all sufficiently in all things, may abound to every good work|In omnibus semper omnem sufficientiam habentes, abundetis in omne opus bonum]].

paras.t: — Sed quum omnes justitiæ nostræ, Isaia testante, sint quasi pannus menstruatæ, quomodo possumus in vita hac in nullo esse deficientes? Et respondendum, quod in his quæ sunt de necessitate salutis, et secundum statum præsentis peregrinationis, homines virtuosi dicuntur in nullo deficere : quemadmodum loquitur et Propheta, Nihil deest timentibus Deum. Corinthiis quoque scribit Apostolus : In omnibus divites facti estis in Christo, ita ut nihil vobis desit in ulla gratia.
paras.en: — But since, as Isaias testifies, [[Is 64:6|all our justices|omnes justitiæ nostræ]] are [[Is 64:6|as the rag of a menstruous woman|quasi pannus menstruatæ]], how can we in this life be [[1:4|failing in nothing|in nullo esse deficientes?]]? The answer is that in the things that are necessary for salvation, and according to the state of our present pilgrimage, virtuous men are said to fail in nothing: as the Prophet also says, [[Ps 33:10|there is no want to them that fear him|Nihil deest timentibus Deum]] [Denis's wording, *Nihil deest timentibus Deum*, "nothing is wanting to them that fear God", is freer than the Vulgate's *non est inopia timentibus eum*]. The Apostle also writes to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 1:5|in all things you are made rich|In omnibus divites facti estis]] in Christ, [[1 Cor 1:7|So that nothing is wanting to you in any grace|ita ut nihil vobis desit in ulla gratia]].

paras.t: Denique, sitis perfecti in interiori dispositione, in omni cogitatu et affectione, integri et veraces in verbis, in nullo deficientes in virtutum operibus. Rursus, Sitis perfecti in fide, habendo fidem cum rationibus credendorum et purificatæ mentis intelligentia, integri in spe, non deficientes in caritate. Plenitudo enim legis est dilectio. — Insuper, istud complexum, Ut sitis perfecti et integri, etc., ad totam præinductam exhortationem est referendum. Propterea namque debemus omne gaudium æstimare, quum in varias inciderimus tentationes, ut simus perfecti et integri, in nullo deficientes.
paras.en: Lastly: [[1:4|be perfect|sitis perfecti]] in your inner disposition, in every thought and affection; [[1:4|entire|integri]] and truthful in words; [[1:4|failing in nothing|in nullo deficientes]] in the works of the virtues. Again: be perfect in faith, having faith together with the reasons for the things to be believed and the understanding of a purified mind; entire in hope; not failing in charity. For [[Rom 13:10|Love therefore is the fulfilling of the law|Plenitudo enim legis est dilectio]]. — Moreover, this whole phrase, [[1:4|that you may be perfect and entire|Ut sitis perfecti et integri]], etc., is to be referred to the whole exhortation that went before. For we ought to count it all joy when we fall into divers temptations for this reason, that we may be perfect and entire, failing in nothing.

paras.t: Et quia ad intelligendum quam fructuosa sit homini varia tribulatio in præsenti, atque ad discernendum inter bonum et malum, inter verum et falsum, indiget homo illuminatione divina, subjungitur : Si, pro quia, quis, imo quicumque vestrum indiget sapientia, id est discretione et intelligentia pertinentium ad salutem, ac notitia Scripturarum, seu dono sapientiæ, quo per gustum internum bene sentit ac judicat homo de Deo. Hac multiplici sapientia omnes jugiter indigemus, præsertim in dubiis, arduis et obscuris : in quibus quid postulemus sicut oportet, nescimus. Propter quod scriptum est : Cogitationes mortalium timidæ, et incertæ providentiæ nostræ. In Job quoque fertur : Nos quippe involvimur tenebris. Postulet a Deo. Omnis enim sapientia a Domino Deo est : ad quem tanquam ad benignissimum patrem, infallibilem directorem, omnipotentem adjutorem, in omni necessitate debemus confugere, quia non deest nec deficit confugientibus ad se. Juxta quod in Ecclesiastico asseritur : Nullus enim speravit in Domino, et confusus est; aut quis invocavit illum, et despexit eum? Quum enim (teste Philosopho) natura non deficiat in necessariis, multo minus Creator, naturæ auctor, in necessariis deficit.
paras.en: And since, to understand how fruitful manifold tribulation is to man in this present life, and to distinguish between good and evil, between true and false, man needs divine enlightenment, there is added: [[1:5|if|Si]] (put for *since*) [[1:5|any|quis]], nay whosoever, [[1:5|of you want wisdom|vestrum indiget sapientia]], that is, discernment and understanding of the things that pertain to salvation, and knowledge of the Scriptures, or the gift of wisdom, by which, through an inward taste, a man thinks and judges rightly of God. Of this manifold wisdom we all stand in constant need, above all in matters doubtful, hard and obscure, in which we know not what we should ask as we ought. For which reason it is written: [[Wis 9:14|the thoughts of mortal men are fearful, and our counsels uncertain|Cogitationes mortalium timidæ, et incertæ providentiæ nostræ]]. In Job too it is said: [[Job 37:19|we are wrapped up in darkness|Nos quippe involvimur tenebris]]. [[1:5|Let him ask of God|Postulet a Deo]]. For all wisdom is from the Lord God; and to him, as to a most kindly father, an unerring guide and an almighty helper, we ought to flee in every need, for he is not wanting to those who flee to him, nor does he fail them. As is declared in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 2:11|no one hath hoped in the Lord, and hath been confounded|Nullus enim speravit in Domino, et confusus est]]; [[Ecclus 2:12|or who hath called upon him, and he despised him?|aut quis invocavit illum, et despexit eum?]] For since (as the Philosopher witnesses) nature does not fail in what is necessary, much less does the Creator, the author of nature, fail in what is necessary.

paras.t: Qui dat omnibus affluenter, id est liberaliter et abunde. Ipse etenim abundantia suæ pietatis merita supplicum excedit et vota; et sicut infinita est bonitas ac opulentia Dei, sic infinita est munificentia ejus. Qui, ut divinus Dionysius docet, per omnem naturæ vultum sua dona diffundit, nec aliquid exsistentium suæ bonitatis communicatione expers relinquit, et unicuique secundum suam capacitatem dispositionemque influit. Omnibus quippe dat dona naturæ, necessaria vitæ; atque ad dandum dona gratiæ semper exhibet se paratum, dummodo quod in se est, faciat homo. Imo quosdam gratiosissime prævenit, et omnem gratiæ obicem ac cordis duritiam tollit ab eis, gratiamque largitur eisdem, non solum supra eorum merita, sed et contra eorum demerita. — Sed objici potest, quod multi sunt pauperes, et in naturalibus etiam defectuosi, et omni gratiarum carentes charismate. Quomodo ergo dat omnibus affluenter, præsertim quum aliqui moriantur ex fame? Et respondendum, quod Deus non dat omnibus æque affluenter; et quod unicuique dat quælibet munera abundanter, sed uni hoc, alteri illud. Et tamen omnibus tribuit dona aliqua affluenter in proprio genere, suoque tempore, quemadmodum scriptum est : Aperis tu manum tuam, et implés omne animal benedictione. Suo etiam tempore ex rationabili causa subtrahit dona sua, sicut ait Psalmista : Omnia a te exspectant, ut des illis escam in tempore. Dante te illis, colligent; aperiente te manum tuam, omnia adimplebuntur bonitate; avertente autem te faciem, turbabuntur; auferes spiritum eorum, et deficient, et in pulverem suum revertentur.
paras.en: [[1:5|who giveth to all men abundantly|Qui dat omnibus affluenter]], that is, liberally and plentifully. For by the abundance of his kindness he goes beyond both the merits and the prayers of those who ask; and as the goodness and riches of God are infinite, so is his bounty infinite. As the divine Dionysius teaches, he pours out his gifts over the whole face of nature, leaves nothing that exists without a share in his goodness, and flows into each thing according to its capacity and disposition. To all, indeed, he gives the gifts of nature, the necessities of life; and he shows himself ever ready to give the gifts of grace, provided that man does what is in him. Nay, some he goes before most graciously, takes away from them every obstacle to grace and all hardness of heart, and bestows grace upon them, not only beyond their merits but even against their demerits. — But it may be objected that many are poor, and lacking even in natural things, and without any charism of graces. How then is he one who [[1:5|giveth to all men abundantly|dat omnibus affluenter]], above all since some die of hunger? The answer is that God does not give to all equally abundantly, nor does he give every gift abundantly to each, but this to one, that to another. And yet to all he grants some gifts abundantly, each in its own kind and in its own time, as it is written: [[Ps 144:16|Thou openest thy hand, and fillest with blessing every living creature.|Aperis tu manum tuam, et implés omne animal benedictione]] And in his own time, for a reasonable cause, he also withdraws his gifts, as the Psalmist says: [[Ps 103:27|All expect of thee that thou give them food in season.|Omnia a te exspectant, ut des illis escam in tempore]] [[Ps 103:28|What thou givest to them they shall gather up: when thou openest thy hand, they shall all be filled with good.|Dante te illis, colligent; aperiente te manum tuam, omnia adimplebuntur bonitate]] [[Ps 103:29|But if thou turnest away thy face, they shall be troubled: thou shalt take away their breath, and they shall fail, and shall return to their dust.|avertente autem te faciem, turbabuntur; auferes spiritum eorum, et deficient, et in pulverem suum revertentur]]

paras.t: Et non improperat. Nonne Deus per Moysen et Prophetas filiis Israel sæpissime improperavit beneficia quæ eis impendit? Nonne etiam Deus ingratitudinem hominum graviter punit, et quotidie per se et suos ministros reprehendit eos de ingratitudine sua? Unde per Moysen ait de filiis Israel : Usquequo multitudo hæc pessima non credet mihi in omnibus mirabilibus meis quæ feci coram eis? Et alibi : Filios, inquit, enutrivi et exaltavi, ipsi autem spreverunt me. Sic et in libris Regum impiis regibus Israelis legitur improperasse, quod elevavit eos de pulvere, et reges constituit populi sui, ipsi vero nequiter egerunt : imo et per Nathan improperavit regi David beneficia sua, quum adulterium homicidiumque fecisset. Quomodo ergo Deus non improperat muneratis a se, beneficia eis collata? Et respondendum, quod Deus, quantum est ex parte suæ bonitatis, invariabilitatis ac sapientiæ, non improperat eis ; sed propter eorum abusiones atque demerita facit hoc, exigente sua justitia. Ingratis ergo improperat, gratis vero majora largitur, prout Christus disseruit : Habenti dabitur, et abundabit ; ei autem qui non habet, et quod videtur habere, auferetur ab eo.
paras.en: [[1:5|and upbraideth not|Et non improperat]] [*improperare*: to reproach someone with a benefit, to cast it in his teeth]. Did not God, through Moses and the Prophets, very often upbraid the children of Israel with the benefits he had bestowed on them? Does not God also punish men's ingratitude severely, and daily rebuke them for their ingratitude, by himself and by his ministers? Thus through Moses he says of the children of Israel: How long will [[Num 14:27|this wicked multitude|multitudo hæc pessima]] [[Num 14:11|not believe me for all the signs that I have wrought before them?|non credet mihi in omnibus mirabilibus meis quæ feci coram eis?]] [Denis joins the words "this wicked multitude" of Num 14:27 to Num 14:11, and has "my wonders" for "the signs".] And elsewhere: [[Is 1:2|I have brought up children|Filios]], he says, [[Is 1:2|and exalted them: but they have despised me|enutrivi et exaltavi, ipsi autem spreverunt me]]. So too in the books of Kings he is read to have upbraided the wicked kings of Israel, that he had raised them up from the dust and made them kings of his people, and they had acted wickedly[[3 Kings 16:2||]]; nay, through Nathan he upbraided King David with his benefits when he had committed adultery and murder[[2 Kings 12:7||]]. How then is it true that God [[1:5|upbraideth not|non improperat]] those he has endowed, with the benefits conferred on them? The answer is that God, so far as concerns his goodness, unchangeableness and wisdom, does not upbraid them; but he does this because of their abuses and demerits, as his justice requires. The ungrateful, then, he upbraids, but on the grateful he bestows yet greater things, as Christ declared: [[Matt 25:29|to every one that hath shall be given, and he shall abound: but from him that hath not, that also which he seemeth to have shall be taken away|Habenti dabitur, et abundabit ; ei autem qui non habet, et quod videtur habere, auferetur ab eo]].

paras.t: Et dabitur ei sapientia a Deo, si fideliter ac perseveranter petierit. Ideo subditur : Postulet autem in fide nihil hæsitans. Quod ait, In fide, referri potest ad verbum, Postulet, et ad participium, Hæsitans. Si referatur ad postulationem, sensus est, ut Deum roget fideliter, secundum veræ fidei directionem. Quum enim fides sit totius spiritualis ædificii fundamentum, oportet in primis ut simus firmi in fide, et certi de veritate ipsius. Fides vero est interior oculus mentis, finem ultimum ad quem ordinanda sunt cetera, ei ostendens, ipsamque dirigens in petendis. Imo omnes actus nostri ex fide procedere debent, et ad supernaturalem beatitudinem, quam fides docet ac monstrat, referri : præsertim quum ad Romanos scribat Apostolus, Omne quod non est ex fide, peccatum est. Sic ergo in fide postulet Deum, nihil hæsitans, id est de misericordia Dei et gratiosa ejus exauditione nihil ambigens nec diffidens. — Porro, si referatur ad hæsitationem, sensus est, ut postulet Deum nihil dubitans de fidei veritate, sed firmus et certus in ea. Habet siquidem fides certitudinem adhærentiæ, quamvis non evidentiæ. Habet quoque certitudinem ex parte objecti, videlicet æternæ et infallibilis veritatis cui innitur, quamvis non omnifarie ex parte subjecti, puta intellectus humani, cujus capacitatem excedunt fidei veritates in vita præsenti.
paras.en: [[1:5|And it shall be given him|Et dabitur ei]], wisdom shall be given him by God, if he ask faithfully and perseveringly. Therefore it is added: [[1:6|But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering|Postulet autem in fide nihil hæsitans]]. The words [[1:6|in faith|in fide]] can be referred to the verb [[1:6|ask|Postulet]] and to the participle [[1:6|wavering|Hæsitans]]. If they are referred to the asking, the sense is that he should pray to God faithfully, according to the guidance of the true faith. For since faith is the foundation of the whole spiritual building, we must first of all be firm in the faith and certain of its truth. Faith is the inward eye of the mind, which shows it the last end to which all else is to be ordered, and guides it in what it asks. Nay, all our acts ought to proceed from faith and be referred to the supernatural beatitude which faith teaches and points out; above all since the Apostle writes to the Romans: [[Rom 14:23|all that is not of faith is sin|Omne quod non est ex fide, peccatum est]]. So then let him ask God in faith, [[1:6|nothing wavering|nihil hæsitans]], that is, in no way doubting or distrusting the mercy of God and his gracious hearing. — But if they are referred to the wavering, the sense is that he should ask God without any doubt about the truth of the faith, but firm and certain in it. For faith has the certitude of adherence, though not of evidence [that is, the believer holds to it with complete firmness, though he does not see its truth]. It has certitude also on the side of its object, namely the eternal and unerring truth on which it rests, though not in every way on the side of the subject, that is, the human understanding, whose capacity the truths of faith exceed in the present life.

paras.t: Quotidie ergo, imo omni hora, Deum devotissime deprecemur, ut mentem nostram jugiter illuminare, dirigere, roborare dignetur, cum Propheta orantes : Deus meus, illumina tenebras meas ; et, Gressus meos dirige secundum eloquium tuum, et non dominetur mei omnis injustitia ; itemque, Illustra faciem tuam super servum tuum. Beatus etenim homo quem tu erudieris, Domine, et de lege tua docueris eum. Atque, ut Salomon ubertim testatur, Dei est mentem docere. Unde et in Proverbiis habetur : Dominus dat sapientiam, et ex ore ejus prudentia et scientia. Nullus itaque de sua præsumat peritia, sed summæ sapientiæ innitatur directioni, quum scriptum sit : Habe fiduciam in Domino ex toto corde tuo, et ne innitaris prudentiæ tuæ. Denique illuminationem divinam invocare oportet cum omni aviditate, diligentia atque instantia, prout Salomon loquitur : Si sapientiam invocaveris, et quæsieris eam quasi pecuniam, et quasi thesauros effoderis eam, tunc scientiam Dei invenies. Verumtamen non sic debemus pro sapientia Deum adorare, ut negligamus a proximis et prælatis ac doctoribus informationem expetere. Sed et angelum sui custodem unusquisque debet quotidie invocare, ut se illustrare, dirigere ac tueri dignetur.
paras.en: Daily, then, nay every hour, let us most devoutly beseech God that he deign continually to enlighten, guide and strengthen our mind, praying with the Prophet: [[Ps 17:29|O my God, enlighten my darkness|Deus meus, illumina tenebras meas]] [the margin gives Ps. xxvii, 20; the words are Ps 17:29]; and, [[Ps 118:133|Direct my steps according to thy word: and let no iniquity have dominion over me.|Gressus meos dirige secundum eloquium tuum, et non dominetur mei omnis injustitia]]; and again, [[Ps 30:17|Make thy face to shine upon thy servant|Illustra faciem tuam super servum tuum]]. For indeed, [[Ps 93:12|Blessed is the man whom thou shalt instruct, O Lord: and shalt teach him out of thy law|Beatus etenim homo quem tu erudieris, Domine, et de lege tua docueris eum]] [the margin gives Ps. xcii, 12; the verse is Ps 93:12]. And, as Solomon abundantly testifies, it belongs to God to teach the mind. Hence in Proverbs too we have: [[Prov 2:6|the Lord giveth wisdom: and out of his mouth cometh prudence and knowledge|Dominus dat sapientiam, et ex ore ejus prudentia et scientia]]. Let no one, then, presume upon his own skill, but let him lean on the guidance of the supreme Wisdom, since it is written: [[Prov 3:5|Have confidence in the Lord with all thy heart, and lean not upon thy own prudence.|Habe fiduciam in Domino ex toto corde tuo, et ne innitaris prudentiæ tuæ]] Lastly, we must call upon the divine enlightenment with all eagerness, diligence and earnestness, as Solomon says: [[Prov 2:3|if thou shalt call for wisdom|Si sapientiam invocaveris]], if [[Prov 2:4|thou shalt seek her as money, and shalt dig for her as for a treasure|et quæsieris eam quasi pecuniam, et quasi thesauros effoderis eam]], then thou [[Prov 2:5|shalt find the knowledge of God|scientiam Dei invenies]]. Yet we must not so pray to God for wisdom as to neglect to seek instruction from our neighbours, our prelates and teachers. And each one ought also to call daily upon his guardian angel, that he deign to enlighten, guide and protect him.

paras.t: Præterea quæri potest, quomodo debeamus Deum orare in fide, nihil hæsitantes de auditione ejus benigna, quum ignoremus an simus in caritate et digni amore : imo præsumptuosum videtur, ut quis præsupponat se exaudiendum a Deo, quem tam graviter totiesque offendit. Et respondendum, quod quæstio ista inquirit qualiter spes nostra ad Deum certitudinem sortiatur, et qualiter non. Spes quippe dicitur, certa exspectatio futuræ beatitudinis. Ad quod Thomas respondet, quod spes certitudinem habet ex parte misericordiæ et omnipotentiæ Dei, cui innititur, et ex qua non erit defectus nostræ salutis. Sed ex consideratione propriæ fragilitatis et dispositionis, habet timorem et incertitudinem quamdam. Unde spes et timor dicuntur duæ molæ, inter quas quotidie spiritualiter moli debemus : ut ex consideratione divinæ pietatis confidamus de meliori, et ex consideratione propriæ imperfectionis labilitatisque vereamur jugiter de pejori, ac de periculo simus suspecti : ut sit spes mola superior, et timor mola inferior. Sic in proposito, quando oramus, debemus sine hæsitatione orare ex consideratione veritatis ac pietatis Altissimi, qui frequenter in Scripturis se promittit exauditurum orantes, dummodo scilicet orent sicut oportet : qui et omnipotens, piissimus, liberalissimus, atque ditissimus est ad dandum. Sed ex consideratione propriæ dispositionis, insufficientiæ, imperfectionis aut culpæ, bonum est formidare, et cum timore ac tremore orare. Hinc Beda circa verba præhabita, Postulet in fide nihil hæsitans, ait : Hoc est, talem se exhibeat bene vivendo, ut dignus sit exaudiri dum postulat. Qui enim meminit se non obtemperasse Dei præceptis, merito hæsitat, quoniam scriptum est : Qui obturat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis. Hinc de quibusdam loquitur Deus : Tunc invocabunt me, et non exaudiam. Atque in libro Job legitur : Numquid Deus exaudiet vocem hypocritæ, quum venerit super eum angustia?
paras.en: It may further be asked how we ought to pray to God in faith, nothing wavering as to his kindly hearing, when we do not know whether we are in charity and worthy of love; nay, it seems presumptuous for anyone to take for granted that he will be heard by God, whom he has offended so gravely and so often. The answer is that this question asks how far our hope in God has certainty, and how far it has not. For hope is called the certain expectation of future beatitude. To which Thomas answers that hope has certainty on the side of the mercy and omnipotence of God, on which it rests, and from which there will be no failure of our salvation; but from the consideration of our own frailty and disposition it has fear and a certain uncertainty. Hence hope and fear are called the two millstones between which we must daily be ground spiritually: so that from the consideration of the divine kindness we may trust for the better, and from the consideration of our own imperfection and proneness to fall we may continually fear the worse and be wary of danger; hope being the upper millstone and fear the lower. So in the matter before us: when we pray, we ought to pray without wavering from the consideration of the truth and kindness of the Most High, who often in the Scriptures promises that he will hear those who pray, provided, that is, that they pray as they ought; who is also almighty, most kind, most liberal and most rich in giving. But from the consideration of our own disposition, insufficiency, imperfection or guilt, it is good to be afraid, and to pray with fear and trembling. Hence Bede, on the words cited above, [[1:6|let him ask in faith, nothing wavering|Postulet in fide nihil hæsitans]], says: That is, let him show himself such by living well that he may be worthy to be heard when he asks. For he who remembers that he has not obeyed God's commandments rightly wavers, since it is written: [[Prov 28:9|He that turneth away his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be an abomination.|Qui obturat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis]] [Bede's wording has "stoppeth his ear" for "turneth away his ears"]. Hence God says of some: [[Prov 1:28|Then shall they call upon me, and I will not hear|Tunc invocabunt me, et non exaudiam]]. And in the book of Job we read: [[Job 27:9|Will God hear his cry, when distress shall come upon him?|Numquid Deus exaudiet vocem hypocritæ, quum venerit super eum angustia?]] [Denis has "the voice of the hypocrite" for "his cry", taking the hypocrite from Job 27:8].

paras.t: Qui enim hæsitat de fidei veritate, aut de misericordia Dei, similis est fluctui maris, qui fluctuatus a vento movetur et circumfertur, id est, mente omnino instabilis est, non fixus in Deo. Errores namque, vitia et impetus passionum, instabilem reddunt mentem, et exauditione indignam, quum nec sincere, nec fixe cohæreat Deo. Maxime autem prætacta hæsitatio de fidei veritate ac pietate divina, est evitanda. Hinc scriptum est : Impii quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest. In Job quoque : Si iniquitatem quæ est in manu tua, abstuleris, tunc levare poteris faciem tuam absque macula, et eris stabilis, et non timebis. Et in Psalmo : Non sic impii, non sic, sed tanquam pulvis quem projicit ventus a facie terræ ; et denuo, In circuitu impii ambulant : siquidem undique evagantur.
paras.en: [[1:6|For he that wavereth|Qui enim hæsitat]] about the truth of the faith or about the mercy of God [[1:6|is like a wave of the sea|similis est fluctui maris]], which, being tossed, [[1:6|is moved and carried about by the wind|a vento movetur et circumfertur]]: that is, he is wholly unstable in mind, not fixed in God. For errors, vices and the onrush of the passions make the mind unstable and unworthy to be heard, since it cleaves to God neither sincerely nor firmly. Above all, the wavering spoken of above, about the truth of the faith and the divine kindness, is to be avoided. Hence it is written: [[Is 57:20|the wicked are like the raging sea, which cannot rest|Impii quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest]]. In Job too: [[Job 11:14|If thou wilt put away from thee the iniquity that is in thy hand|Si iniquitatem quæ est in manu tua, abstuleris]], [[Job 11:15|Then mayst thou lift up thy face without spot, and thou shalt be steadfast, and shalt not fear.|tunc levare poteris faciem tuam absque macula, et eris stabilis, et non timebis]] And in the Psalm: [[Ps 1:4|Not so the wicked, not so: but like the dust, which the wind driveth from the face of the earth.|Non sic impii, non sic, sed tanquam pulvis quem projicit ventus a facie terræ]]; and again, [[Ps 11:9|The wicked walk round about|In circuitu impii ambulant]], since they wander off on every side.

paras.t: Non ergo æstimet homo ille sic hæsitans, quod accipiat aliquid, id est aliquod donum gratiæ gratum facientis, a Domino, qui naturalia et temporalia bona ac dona gratiæ gratis datæ tribuit bonis et malis, reprobis et electis. Talis ergo, quamdiu permanet talis, non exauditur, quantum ad dona pertinentia ad salutem, juxta illud, Scimus quoniam Deus peccatores non audit : qui scilicet in peccandi manent proposito. Unde et in Threnis dicitur Deo : Nos inique egimus, et te ad iracundiam provocavimus, idcirco tu inexorabilis es. Verumtamen, si talis pœniteat, seque disponat ad gratiam, faciens quod in se est, Deus clementer eum exaudit. Propter quod rursus ibidem fertur : Scrutemur vias nostras, et quæramus, et revertamur ad Dominum. Levemus corda nostra cum manibus ad Dominum in cœlos, quia non repellet in sempiternum Dominus : quia etsi abjecit, miserebitur secundum multitudinem misericordiæ suæ.
paras.en: [[1:7|Therefore let not that man think|Non ergo æstimet homo ille]], wavering thus, [[1:7|that he shall receive any thing|quod accipiat aliquid]], that is, any gift of sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes a man pleasing to God], [[1:7|of the Lord|a Domino]], who bestows natural and temporal goods, and the gifts of grace freely given [*gratia gratis data*, gifts such as prophecy or miracles, given for the good of others and not making the receiver holy], on good and bad, reprobate and elect alike. Such a man, then, so long as he remains such, is not heard as regards the gifts that pertain to salvation, according to that saying: [[John 9:31|we know that God doth not hear sinners|Scimus quoniam Deus peccatores non audit]]; those, that is, who remain in the purpose of sinning. Hence in Lamentations too it is said to God: [[Lam 3:42|We have done wickedly, and provoked thee to wrath: therefore thou art inexorable|Nos inique egimus, et te ad iracundiam provocavimus, idcirco tu inexorabilis es]]. Yet if such a man repents and disposes himself for grace, doing what is in him, God mercifully hears him. For which reason it is said again in the same place: [[Lam 3:40|Let us search our ways, and seek, and return to the Lord|Scrutemur vias nostras, et quæramus, et revertamur ad Dominum]]. [[Lam 3:41|Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to the Lord in the heavens|Levemus corda nostra cum manibus ad Dominum in cœlos]], [[Lam 3:31|For the Lord will not cast off for ever|quia non repellet in sempiternum Dominus]]: [[Lam 3:32|For if he hath cast off, he will also have mercy, according to the multitude of his mercies|quia etsi abjecit, miserebitur secundum multitudinem misericordiæ suæ]].

paras.t: Ut ergo mereamur desuper exaudiri, studeamus in veritatis cognitione et bonitatis amore constabiliri, in fide, spe et caritate firmari, in salutari sapientia radicari : ne passionibus exagitetur cor nostrum, nec seducamur erroribus, sed in omni eventu perseveremus fixi in Deo, quemadmodum hortatur Apostolus : Jam non simus parvuli fluctuantes, nec circumferamur omni vento doctrinæ, in nequitia hominum, in astutia, ad circumventionem erroris.
