Further, since the sacrament of Penance is the second plank after shipwreck, regenerating us, so this is also done daily in the sacrament of Penance. And since Christ, the incarnate Word of the Father, instituted the sacraments of the gospel law, it can be understood that the Father has regenerated us in the aforesaid ways by the Word of truth, that is, through His eternal and uncreated Word, which is truth itself.

paras.t: Hæc autem fecit Deus voluntarie, non coacte aut necessitate naturæ, sicut per Osee testatur : Diligam eos spontanee. Et teste Apostolo, Deus operatur omnia secundum consilium voluntatis suæ. Per quod refutatur error quorumdam philosophorum et hæreticorum, qui asseruerunt processionem creaturarum a Creatore esse naturalem emicationem ac emanationem, non liberam. Contra quos etiam Plato ait in primo Timæi : Optimus erat Deus. Porro ab optimo longe relegata est omnis invidia. Voluit ergo Deus omnia suæ bonitatis aut beatitudinis esse participia : quam quidem Dei voluntatem si quis rerum principium dixerit, recte eum putare consentiam.
paras.en: Now God did these things of His own will, not under compulsion or by necessity of nature, as He testifies through Osee: [[Osee 14:5|I will love them freely|Diligam eos spontanee]]. And, as the Apostle witnesses, God [[Eph 1:11|worketh all things according to the counsel of his will|operatur omnia secundum consilium voluntatis suæ]]. By this is refuted the error of certain philosophers and heretics who asserted that the procession of creatures from the Creator is a natural outflashing and emanation, not a free one. Against whom Plato too says in the first book of the Timæus: God was most good; and from the most good all envy is far banished. God therefore willed all things to be sharers of His goodness or beatitude; and if anyone should call this will of God the principle of things, I will agree that he judges rightly.

paras.t: Sic ergo nos genuit, ut simus initium aliquod creaturæ ejus, id est, inter corporales ipsius creaturas habeamus primatum : quibus non solum per dona gratiæ, imo et per dona naturæ præferimur. Propter quod dixit Deus : Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram ; et præsit piscibus maris, et volatilibus cœli, et bestiis terræ, universæque creaturæ. Moyses quoque : Solem et lunam et omnia astra creavit Deus in ministerium cunctis gentibus. Porro, per dona gratiæ Christiani ceteris omnibus mundi hominibus incomparabiliter præferuntur, quum sint adoptivi filii Dei, et ejus heredes, et Christi membra ac coheredes. Et ipsi soli sunt in statu salutis, ceteri omnes in statu damnationis, suntque membra, filii ac ministri diaboli. Præterea, quod loquitur Moyses de excellentia populi Israelitici ad Deum tunc pertinentis, dicendo, Non est alia natio tam grandis ; itemque, Quæ est gens una in terra sic inclyta, etc. ? nunc multo præclarius dici potest de populo veraciter christiano, de quo princeps Apostolorum testatur : Vos genus electum, regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus acquisitionis. Sed, proh dolor ! homo quum in honore esset, non intellexit, et multi Christianorum gentilibus deterius vivunt. Postremo, pro eo quod hic dicitur, Ut simus initium aliquod creaturæ ejus, alia littera continet : Ut simus primitiæ creaturarum ejus. Primitias namque frugum et animalium jussit lex Domino consecrari, id est optima quæque in frugibus ac animantibus. Ita et Deus verbo veritatis nos genuit, ut inter omnes homines simus optimus populus ejus.
paras.en: So then He begot us, [[1:18|that we might be some beginning of his creature|ut simus initium aliquod creaturæ ejus]], that is, that we might have the primacy among His bodily creatures, above which we are preferred not only by the gifts of grace but also by the gifts of nature. Therefore God said: [[Gen 1:26|Let us make man to our image and likeness: and let him have dominion over the fishes of the sea, and the fowls of the air, and the beasts, and the whole earth|Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram ; et præsit piscibus maris, et volatilibus cœli, et bestiis terræ, universæque creaturæ]] [Denis has *and every creature* for *the whole earth*]. Moses also says that God created the sun and moon and all the stars for the service of all nations[[Deut 4:19||]]. Further, by the gifts of grace Christians are incomparably preferred to all other men of the world, since they are adopted sons of God, and His heirs, and members and joint heirs of Christ[[Rom 8:17||]]. And they alone are in the state of salvation; all the others are in the state of damnation, and are members, sons and ministers of the devil. Moreover, what Moses says of the excellence of the people of Israel, which then belonged to God, saying: [[Deut 4:7|Neither is there any other nation so great|Non est alia natio tam grandis]]; and again: [[Deut 4:8|what other nation is there so renowned|Quæ est gens una in terra sic inclyta]], etc.? can now be said much more gloriously of the truly Christian people, of whom the prince of the Apostles testifies: [[1 Pet 2:9|you are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation, a purchased people|Vos genus electum, regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus acquisitionis]]. But, alas! [[Ps 48:13|man when he was in honour did not understand|homo quum in honore esset, non intellexit]], and many Christians live worse than the heathen. Lastly, for what is said here, That we might be some beginning of his creature, another reading has: That we might be the firstfruits of his creatures. For the law commanded the firstfruits of crops and of animals to be consecrated to the Lord, that is, all the best among crops and animals. So also God begot us by the word of truth, that among all men we might be His best people.

paras.t: Scitis, fratres mei dilectissimi, id est, notum vobis est, universa quæ scribo esse verissima, quia scitis Apostolos primitias accepisse Spiritus Sancti. Verumtamen non sufficit vobis hoc scire. Ideo subditur : Sit autem omnis homo velox ad audiendum verba salutis. Beati enim qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud; et, Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit. Idcirco, ut in Ecclesiastico dicitur. Auris bona cum omni concupiscentia audiet sapientiam. Tardus autem ad loquendum : quia hoc sapientiæ signum est, eo quod Salomone testante, in multiloquio non desit peccatum. Atque idem alibi : Totum spiritum suum profert stultus; sapiens differt et reservat in posterum. Et denuo : Vidisti aliquem velocem ad loquendum? Stultitia magis speranda est, quam illius correctio. In Ecclesiastico quoque legitur : Qui multis utitur verbis, lædit animam suam.
paras.en: [[1:19|You know, my dearest brethren|Scitis, fratres mei dilectissimi]], that is, it is known to you that all I write is most true, for you know that the Apostles received the firstfruits of the Holy Ghost[[Rom 8:23||]]. But it is not enough for you to know this. Therefore he adds: [[1:19|And let every man be swift to hear|Sit autem omnis homo velox ad audiendum]] the words of salvation. For [[Luke 11:28|blessed are they who hear the word of God and keep it|Beati enim qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud]]; and: [[John 8:47|He that is of God heareth the words of God|Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit]]. Therefore, as is said in Ecclesiasticus, [[Ecclus 3:31|a good ear will hear wisdom with all desire|Auris bona cum omni concupiscentia audiet sapientiam]]. [[1:19|but slow to speak|Tardus autem ad loquendum]]: for this is a sign of wisdom, since, as Solomon testifies, [[Prov 10:19|In the multitude of words there shall not want sin|in multiloquio non desit peccatum]]. And the same elsewhere: [[Prov 29:11|A fool uttereth all his mind: a wise man deferreth, and keepeth it till afterwards|Totum spiritum suum profert stultus; sapiens differt et reservat in posterum]]. And again: [[Prov 29:20|Hast thou seen a man hasty to speak? folly is rather to be looked for, than his amendment|Vidisti aliquem velocem ad loquendum? Stultitia magis speranda est, quam illius correctio]]. In Ecclesiasticus too we read: [[Ecclus 20:8|He that useth many words shall hurt his own soul|Qui multis utitur verbis, lædit animam suam]].

paras.t: Verumtamen in omnibus istis necessaria valde est discretio, ut sit homo quantum in se est, velox ad audiendum, et tardus ad loquendum : quod tamen ad juniores ac subditos et indoctos potissimum pertinet. Nihilo minus, causa rationabili exigente, sit homo velox ad loquendum, præsertim qui præest, dum fraterna correptio aut justa correctio sunt delinquentibus impendendæ, dum etiam proximus indiget informatione, aut revocatione a culpa atque periculis quibus appropinquat. Ideo Salomon dixit : Tempus loquendi, et tempus tacendi est. Atque in Ecclesiastico dicitur : Est tacens, qui invenitur sapiens; est autem tacens, non habens sensum loquelæ; et est tacens, sciens tempus aptum. Homo sapiens tacebit usque ad tempus; lascivus et imprudens non servabit tempus. Sic et juniores ac subditi et indocti, dum ex ignorantia sibi periculum vident instare, mox seniores, sapientiores et superiores suos debent interrogare, et eos cum omni reverentia ac aviditate audire, juxta illud : In multitudine presbyterorum prudentium sta, et sapientiæ illorum ex corde conjungere. Hinc alibi dicitur : Non te prætereat narratio seniorum. Denique, quam salubre est verba salutis audire, tam periculosum est verba audire vana, scurrilia, detractoria et iniqua, quæ mentem maculant audientis, si ea libenter audierit, aut eis consenserit. A talibus ergo verbis avertatur auditus, si fieri potest, atque ad minus ratio ea detestetur. Ideo ait Scriptura : Sepi aures tuas spinis, et noli audire linguam nequam. Propheta quoque locutus est Deo : Narraverunt mihi iniqui fabulationes, sed non ut lex tua.
paras.en: Yet in all these things discretion is very necessary, so that a man be, as far as in him lies, swift to hear and slow to speak; which nevertheless belongs chiefly to the younger, to subjects and to the unlearned. Nonetheless, when reasonable cause requires, let a man be swift to speak, especially one who is set over others, when fraternal reproof or just correction must be given to wrongdoers, and when one's neighbour needs instruction, or calling back from sin and from the dangers he is approaching. Therefore Solomon said: [[Eccles 3:7|a time to speak|Tempus loquendi, et tempus tacendi est]]. And in Ecclesiasticus it is said: [[Ecclus 20:5|There is one that holdeth his peace, that is found wise|Est tacens, qui invenitur sapiens]]; [[Ecclus 20:6|There is one that holdeth his peace, because he knoweth not what to say: and there is another that holdeth his peace, knowing the proper time.|est autem tacens, non habens sensum loquelæ; et est tacens, sciens tempus aptum]]. [[Ecclus 20:7|A wise man will hold his peace till he see opportunity: but a babbler, and a fool, will regard no time.|Homo sapiens tacebit usque ad tempus; lascivus et imprudens non servabit tempus]]. So also the younger, subjects and the unlearned, when they see danger threatening them from ignorance, ought at once to ask their elders, the wiser and their superiors, and to hear them with all reverence and eagerness, according to that: [[Ecclus 6:35|Stand in the multitude of ancients that are wise, and join thyself from thy heart to their wisdom|In multitudine presbyterorum prudentium sta, et sapientiæ illorum ex corde conjungere]]. Hence it is said elsewhere: [[Ecclus 8:11|Let not the discourse of the ancients escape thee|Non te prætereat narratio seniorum]]. Further, as wholesome as it is to hear the words of salvation, so dangerous is it to hear vain, scurrilous, detracting and wicked words, which stain the mind of the hearer if he hears them willingly or consents to them. From such words, then, let the hearing be turned away, if it can be done, and at least let reason detest them. Therefore Scripture says: [[Ecclus 28:28|Hedge in thy ears with thorns, hear not a wicked tongue|Sepi aures tuas spinis: linguam nequam]]. The Prophet also spoke to God: [[Ps 118:85|The wicked have told me fables: but not as thy law|Narraverunt mihi iniqui fabulationes, sed non ut lex tua]].

paras.t: Circa hunc locum loquitur Beda : Qui sapientiam diligit, primo postulet eam a Deo, deinde magistrum veritatis humiliter audiat, et inter agendum suam cautissime coerceat linguam. Tutius enim veritas auditur, quam prædicetur. Hinc Pythagorici naturalis scientiæ magisterio præditi, auditores suos per quinquennium jusserunt silere, et postmodum loqui ac docere permiserunt. Unde et Jeremias propheta, bene instructi adolescentis vitam describens, modestiam taciturnitatis inter prima virtutum studia computat : Bonum est, inquiens, viro, quum portaverit jugum ab adolescentia sua ; sedebit solitarius, et tacebit.
paras.en: On this place Bede says: Let him who loves wisdom first ask it of God, then humbly hear the master of truth, and in the meantime most carefully restrain his tongue. For truth is more safely heard than preached. Hence the Pythagoreans, endowed with the mastery of natural science, ordered their hearers to keep silence for five years, and afterwards allowed them to speak and teach. Hence too the prophet Jeremias, describing the life of a well-instructed youth, counts the modesty of silence among the first pursuits of the virtues, saying: [[Lam 3:27|It is good for a man, when he hath borne the yoke from his youth|Bonum est, inquiens, viro, quum portaverit jugum ab adolescentia sua]]; [[Lam 3:28|He shall sit solitary, and hold his peace|sedebit solitarius, et tacebit]].

paras.t: Itaque per prædicta reprehenduntur, qui ad fabulandum, ad docendum, ad prædicandum sunt promptuli, quum nondum in virtutibus exercitati, nondum sufficienter edocti, nondum a vanitatum expurgati vitiis sint. Verumtamen, cui ex officio incumbit docendi aut prædicandi necessitas, studeat se ad exercendum hos actus exhibere idoneum, in virtutibus ac sapientia proficiendo quotidie, et interim quod per se ipsum facere nequit, per alios idoneos faciat.
paras.en: Thus by the foregoing are rebuked those who are quick to chatter, to teach, to preach, when they are not yet exercised in the virtues, not yet sufficiently taught, not yet purged from the vices of vanities. Yet let him on whom the necessity of teaching or preaching falls by office strive to make himself fit to exercise these acts, advancing daily in virtues and wisdom; and meanwhile what he cannot do himself, let him do through other fit persons.

paras.t: Sit quoque omnis homo et tardus ad iram. Ira est appetitus vindictæ propter illatam injuriam. Et ista est duplex : Una, quæ rationem prævenit et excæcat, quæ vocatur ira per vitium, quia ratione non regitur, nec secundum ordinem juris tendit in ultionem. Ad hanc sic tardi esse debemus, ut eam nunquam admittamus : vel si oriri cœperit, statim per rationis censuram mansuetudinisque virtutem frenetur et extinguatur ; vel saltem sic cohibeatur ne per verba aut signa erumpat, neque per inhonestos apparatus pandatur, sicque paulatim suffocetur in semetipsa. Alia est ira per zelum, quæ rationem sequens, sponte assumitur, ut actus virtutis robustius exerceatur. Et ista est bona, quia per eam secundum rationis judicium fit vindicta. Non tamen est passim atque faciliter admittenda, quia et ipsa rationem aliqualiter turbat, secundum Gregorium. Idcirco ad eam tardi esse debemus, et tunc eam assumere quando aliter actus justitiæ tam convenienter exerceri non valet, ut si quis durus incorrigibilisque exsistat. Et hæc ira fuit in Christo, juxta illud : Contristatus est Jesus super cæcitate cordis eorum, circumspiciens eos cum ira. Hinc loquitur Beda : Tardos ad iram nos esse præcepit, ut non ob quaslibet causas, serenitatem nostri cordis ac vultus in austeritatem vertamus ; sed certa exsistente ratione, verbi gratia, si aliter corrigi proximos, maxime eos qui nobis commissi sunt, non posse conspicimus, severitatem verbi aut districtionem judicii erga eos exhibeamus, manente tamen, quantum humana natura patitur, statu nostræ mentis sereno. Sic Phinees, Samuel, Elias et Petrus, tardi fuerunt ad iram, qui tamen peccantes gladio peremerunt aut verbo. Sic et Moyses quum esset vir mitissimus, exivit a Pharaone iratus nimis, comminatus ei pœnam, quam et opere perpetravit ; qui etiam vituli aurei adoratores districte punivit. Hinc teste Gregorio, Ira non debet rationem quasi domina præcedere, sed tanquam ancilla sequi.
paras.en: Let every man also be [[1:19|slow to anger|et tardus ad iram]]. Anger is the desire of vengeance for an injury inflicted. And it is twofold. One kind forestalls reason and blinds it, and is called anger through vice, because it is not ruled by reason and does not tend to vengeance according to the order of right. To this we ought to be so slow as never to admit it; or if it begins to arise, let it at once be bridled and extinguished by the censure of reason and the virtue of meekness; or at least let it be so restrained that it does not break out in words or signs, nor show itself by unseemly displays, and so little by little be stifled in itself. The other is anger through zeal, which, following reason, is taken up deliberately, so that an act of virtue may be exercised more vigorously. And this is good, because through it vengeance is done according to the judgment of reason. Yet it is not to be admitted everywhere and easily, because it too troubles reason somewhat, according to Gregory. Therefore we ought to be slow to it, and take it up only when an act of justice cannot otherwise be so fittingly exercised, as when someone proves hard and incorrigible. And this anger was in Christ, according to that: [[Mark 3:5|looking round about on them with anger, being grieved for the blindness of their hearts|Contristatus est Jesus super cæcitate cordis eorum, circumspiciens eos cum ira]]. Hence Bede says: He commanded us to be slow to anger, so that we do not for any cause whatever turn the serenity of our heart and countenance into severity; but when there is a sure reason, for example, if we see that our neighbours, especially those committed to us, cannot otherwise be corrected, we may show them severity of word or strictness of judgment, while the state of our mind nevertheless remains serene, as far as human nature allows. Thus Phinees[[Num 25:7||]], Samuel[[1 Kings 15:33||]], Elias[[3 Kings 18:40||]] and Peter[[Matt 26:51||]][[Acts 5:1||]] were slow to anger, who yet slew sinners with the sword or with a word. So too Moses, though he was the mildest of men[[Num 12:3||]], went out from Pharao exceeding angry[[Ex 11:8||]] [the margin gives Exod. xi, 9; the words are at 11:8], threatening him with a punishment which he also carried out in deed; who also strictly punished the worshippers of the golden calf[[Ex 32:27||]]. Hence, as Gregory witnesses, anger ought not to go before reason like a mistress, but follow it like a handmaid.

paras.t: Porro ira per vitium, dupliciter fit mortalis : primo, propter commotionis immoderantiam nimis immoderatam, rationemque penitus offuscantem ; secundo, propter ultionis excessum, ut si quis pro illata sibi injuria, exercere cupiat sive exerceat ultionem tam grandem ut directe contrarietur justitiæ. Denique iram Scriptura valde vituperat et condemnat, stultitiam vocat, et iracundum stulto assimilat. Ait namque Salvator : Omnis qui irascitur fratri suo, reus erit judicio. Salomon quoque : Spiritum ad irascendum facilem quis poterit sustinere ? Et iterum Salomon loquitur : Ne sis velox ad irascendum, quoniam ira in sinu stulti requiescit. Et Job : Virum stultum interficit iracundia. Hinc ait Hieronymus : Quid iracundo furor suus confert, quem sævissimis exagitat stimulis ? Sicque ab omni mentis consilio alienat, ut dum irascitur, insanire credatur. Idcirco abbas Agathon dixit : Iracundus homo, etiam si mortuos suscitet, Deo non placet. Imo quam nociva sit ira, pandit Gregorius, dicens : Per iram justitia relinquitur, gratia vitæ socialis amittitur, mansuetudo aufertur, lux veritatis repellitur. Hinc Jacobus subdit :
paras.en: Further, anger through vice becomes mortal in two ways: first, through an excessive immoderation of agitation, wholly darkening reason; secondly, through excess of vengeance, as when someone, for an injury done to him, desires to take or takes a vengeance so great that it is directly contrary to justice. Moreover, Scripture greatly reproves and condemns anger, calls it folly, and likens the angry man to a fool. For the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:22|whosoever is angry with his brother, shall be in danger of the judgment|Omnis qui irascitur fratri suo, reus erit judicio]]. Solomon also: [[Prov 18:14|a spirit that is easily angered, who can bear?|Spiritum ad irascendum facilem quis poterit sustinere]]? And again Solomon says: [[Eccles 7:10|Be not quickly angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of a fool|Ne sis velox ad irascendum, quoniam ira in sinu stulti requiescit]]. And Job: [[Job 5:2|Anger indeed killeth the foolish|Virum stultum interficit iracundia]]. Hence Jerome says: What does his fury profit the angry man, whom it drives on with the cruellest goads? And it so estranges him from all counsel of mind that while he is angry he is thought to be mad. Therefore abbot Agathon said: An angry man, even if he raises the dead, does not please God. Indeed, how harmful anger is Gregory shows, saying: Through anger justice is forsaken, the grace of social life is lost, meekness is taken away, the light of truth is driven back. Hence James adds:

paras.t: Ira enim viri, justitiam Dei non operatur. Sobrie loquitur sanctus ille Apostolus: siquidem minus dicitur, et majus significatur. Ut sit sensus : Ira enim viri, id est ira per vitium cujuscumque hominis, justitiam Dei, id est opus vere justum et Deo acceptum, non operatur, sed opus Deo displicens atque damnabile facit, quia a rationis tramite abducit, et contra justitiam agit. Iracundo quippe bonum et justum videtur, quidquid ab ira suggeritur. Atque, ut ait Gregorius, menti furore ebriæ, quidquid recte dicitur, perversum videtur. Et rursus : Per iram, inquit, sapientia perditur, ut quid, quove ordine quid agendum sit, nesciatur. Hinc Job : Non te ira superet, ut aliquem opprimas. Et Salomon : Ira non habet misericordiam, nec erumpens furor ; et impetum concitati spiritus ferre quis poterit ? Irascamur ergo propriis vitiis, et ea ulciscamur discrete in nobis. Irascere tibi quia ad iram irrationabiliter motus es, et cessa irasci. Et maxime qui vel ex usu maligno aut naturali dispositione ad iram proclives sunt, contra iram jugiter debent pugnare, et pro ejus exstirpatione studere, ac Deum infatigabiliter deprecari. Advertamus ergo quod ait Salvator : Beati mites ; et, Discite a me quia mitis sum et humilis corde.
paras.en: [[1:20|For the anger of man worketh not the justice of God|Ira enim viri, justitiam Dei non operatur]]. That holy Apostle speaks with restraint: for less is said and more is meant. So that the sense is: For the anger of man, that is, the vicious anger of any man whatever, worketh not the justice of God, that is, a work truly just and acceptable to God, but produces a work displeasing to God and damnable, because it leads away from the path of reason and acts against justice. For to the angry man whatever anger suggests seems good and just. And, as Gregory says, to a mind drunk with fury, whatever is rightly said seems perverse. And again: Through anger, he says, wisdom is lost, so that one knows not what is to be done, or in what order. Hence Job: [[Job 36:18|Therefore let not anger overcome thee to oppress any man|Non te ira superet, ut aliquem opprimas]]. And Solomon: [[Prov 27:4|Anger hath no mercy: nor fury, when it breaketh forth: and who can bear the violence of one provoked?|Ira non habet misericordiam, nec erumpens furor ; et impetum concitati spiritus ferre quis poterit]]? Let us then be angry with our own vices, and avenge them discreetly in ourselves. Be angry with thyself because thou wast moved unreasonably to anger, and cease to be angry. And especially those who, whether from bad habit or natural disposition, are prone to anger ought continually to fight against anger, strive for its uprooting, and pray to God untiringly. Let us heed, then, what the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:4|Blessed are the meek|Beati mites]]; and: [[Matt 11:29|learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart|Discite a me quia mitis sum et humilis corde]].

paras.t: Superbi siquidem ad iram sunt proniores : humiles vero mitescunt et patientes consistunt. Denique si ira subito oriatur, nequaquam perseveret in corde, quum in Ecclesiastico dicatur : Homo homini servat iram, et a Deo quærit medelam ? Quis exorabit pro delictis illius ? Insuper, locus iste etiam de ira per zelum potest exponi : quoniam etsi ira hæc commendetur, tamen per eam judicans aut ulciscens, a divinæ perfectionis tranquillitate et summi Judicis serenitate occumbit. Scriptum est enim de Deo : Tu, dominator Domine, cum tranquillitate judicas. Et alibi : Numquid ad iracundiam me provocant ? ait Dominus ; nonne semetipsos in confusione vultus sui ? Hinc asserit Beda : Judex homo, qui amissa mentis tranquillitate judicat delinquentem, etiamsi juste judicet, justitiam tamen divini examinis, in quam perturbatio cadere nequit, imitari non valet.
paras.en: For the proud are more prone to anger, but the humble grow gentle and remain patient. Further, if anger arises suddenly, let it by no means persist in the heart, since it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 28:3|Man to man reserveth anger, and doth he seek remedy of God?|Homo homini servat iram, et a Deo quærit medelam]]? [[Ecclus 28:5|who shall obtain pardon for his sins?|Quis exorabit pro delictis illius]]? Moreover, this place can also be expounded of anger through zeal: for although this anger is commended, yet one who judges or avenges through it falls short of the tranquillity of the divine perfection and the serenity of the supreme Judge. For it is written of God: [[Wis 12:18|thou being master of power, judgest with tranquillity|Tu, dominator Domine, cum tranquillitate judicas]]. And elsewhere: [[Jer 7:19|Do they provoke me to anger, saith the Lord? is it not themselves, to the confusion of their own countenance?|Numquid ad iracundiam me provocant ? ait Dominus ; nonne semetipsos in confusione vultus sui]]? Hence Bede asserts: A human judge who judges an offender having lost the tranquillity of his mind, even if he judges justly, cannot imitate the justice of the divine examination, into which no disturbance can fall.

paras.t: Propter quod abjicientes omnem immunditiam, id est, pœnitendo seu præcavendo, de vobis expellite carnalia ac spiritualia vitia consueta : quemadmodum monet Apostolus, Mundemus nos ab omni inquinamento carnis et spiritus, perficientes sanctificationem in timore Dei ; et abundantiam malitiæ, id est graviora facinora, ut quæ ex consuetudine prava, ex deliberato proposito, ex pertinaci intentione nascuntur ; in mansuetudine suscipite, id est, mansuete et patienter audite, firmiterque tenete, insitum verbum, id est evangelicæ legis doctrinam, vobis a prædicatoribus insinuatam, impressam, infusam. Maturitas enim sapientiæ seu verbum salutaris doctrinæ, non nisi mansuete et tranquilla mente percipitur : a cujus salubri susceptione impedit ira. Idcirco in Ecclesiastico docetur : Esto mansuetus ad audiendum verbum Dei, ut intelligas. Nam ut communiter dicitur, Impedit ira animum ne possit cernere verum. Mansuetudo autem est quædam tractabilitas mentis, eam disponens ad susceptionem verbi salutis : quemadmodum tractabilitas ceræ, dispositio est ad impressionem sigilli.
paras.en: [[1:21|Wherefore, casting away all uncleanness|Propter quod abjicientes omnem immunditiam]], that is, by repenting or guarding against them, drive out from yourselves the carnal and spiritual vices you are used to, as the Apostle admonishes: [[2 Cor 7:1|let us cleanse ourselves from all defilement of the flesh and of the spirit, perfecting sanctification in the fear of God|Mundemus nos ab omni inquinamento carnis et spiritus, perficientes sanctificationem in timore Dei]]; [[1:21|and abundance of naughtiness|et abundantiam malitiæ]], that is, the graver crimes, such as spring from wicked habit, from deliberate purpose, from obstinate intention; [[1:21|with meekness receive|in mansuetudine suscipite]], that is, hear meekly and patiently, and hold firmly, [[1:21|the ingrafted word|insitum verbum]], that is, the teaching of the gospel law, instilled, impressed and poured into you by the preachers. For the ripeness of wisdom, or the word of saving doctrine, is received only with a meek and tranquil mind; from whose wholesome reception anger hinders. Therefore Ecclesiasticus teaches: [[Ecclus 5:13|Be meek to hear the word, that thou mayst understand|Esto mansuetus ad audiendum verbum Dei, ut intelligas]] [Denis's text adds *of God*]. For, as is commonly said, Anger hinders the mind from being able to discern the truth. Meekness is a certain tractableness of mind, disposing it to the reception of the word of salvation, as the tractableness of wax is a disposition for the impression of the seal.

paras.t: Quod potest salvare animas vestras. Nam verbum Dei instruit hominem de necessariis ad salutem, et ita instrumentaliter seu dispositive salvare dicitur hominem, si observetur et impleatur. Ideo dictum est : Beati qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud. Et Psalmista : Lucerna, inquit, pedibus meis verbum tuum, Domine, et lumen semitis meis. Alibi quoque fertur : Non nativitatis fructus pascunt homines, sed sermo tuus eos qui in te credunt, conservat. Cum omni ergo reverentia ac diligentia audiant subditi verbum Dei a superioribus suis ac sapientioribus. Hæc autem purgatio mentis necessaria est, quia oportet in primis a malo recedere. In malevolam enim animam non intrabit sapientia, nec habitabit in corpore subdito peccatis. Itaque puritas mentis est maxime appetenda, jugiter exquirenda, diligentissime conservanda : quia ut ait Salvator, Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt; Salomon quoque, Qui diligit cordis munditiam, habebit amicum regem. Ideo cum Psalmista incessanter oremus : Cor mundum crea in me, Deus.
paras.en: [[1:21|which is able to save your souls|Quod potest salvare animas vestras]]. For the word of God instructs man in the things necessary for salvation, and so it is said to save man instrumentally or dispositively, if it is observed and fulfilled. Therefore it was said: [[Luke 11:28|blessed are they who hear the word of God and keep it|Beati qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud]]. And the Psalmist says: [[Ps 118:105|Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths|Lucerna, inquit, pedibus meis verbum tuum, Domine, et lumen semitis meis]]. Elsewhere too it is said: [[Wis 16:26|not the growing of fruits that nourisheth men, but thy word preserveth them that believe in thee|Non nativitatis fructus pascunt homines, sed sermo tuus eos qui in te credunt, conservat]]. With all reverence and diligence, then, let subjects hear the word of God from their superiors and those wiser than they. Now this purging of the mind is necessary, because we must first of all depart from evil. For [[Wis 1:4|wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins|In malevolam enim animam non intrabit sapientia, nec habitabit in corpore subdito peccatis]]. Therefore purity of mind is above all to be desired, continually sought, most diligently preserved: for, as the Saviour says, [[Matt 5:8|Blessed are the clean of heart: they shall see God|Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt]]; and Solomon: [[Prov 22:11|He that loveth cleanness of heart|Qui diligit cordis munditiam]] shall have the king for his friend. Therefore let us pray unceasingly with the Psalmist: [[Ps 50:12|Create a clean heart in me, O God|Cor mundum crea in me, Deus]].

1.title: ELUCIDATIO RESIDUI HUJUS CAPITULI PRIMI : ESTOTE AUTEM FACTORES VERBI.
1.title_en: Explanation of the rest of this first chapter: But be ye doers of the word.

paras.t: JAM sanctus apostolus Jacobus admonuit, ut omni immunditia atque malitia eradicatis, suscipiamus in mansuetudine insitum verbum Dei. Sed ne putemus nobis sufficere verbum Dei audire, nunc subdit : Estote autem factores verbi, et non auditores tantum, id est, eloquia præceptorum Dei et Ecclesiæ non solum audite, sed et opere implete. Sic et Paulus disseruit : Non auditores legis justi sunt apud Deum, sed factores legis justificabuntur; et Propheta, Intellectus bonus omnibus facientibus eum. Scientia enim moralis ordinatur ad opus. Propter quod dixit Philosophus : Quid est virtus scrutamur, non ut sciamus, sed ut boni efficiamur. Et rursus primo Ethicorum testatur, quod intenti instructioni morali, et eam non exsequentes in opere, similes sunt ægris, medicos diligenter audientibus, sed eorum doctrinam non observantibus. Sic ergo, Estote factores verbi, non auditores tantum, fallentes vosmetipsos : quia qui sola auditione contenti sunt, se ipsos decipiunt : vel formaliter et directe, ut si putent sibi ad salutem sufficere, solum audire et scire; vel concomitanter seu æquivalenter aut materialiter, secundum quod omnis qui peccat, se decipit, juxta illud, Stultus illudit peccatum. Et rursus Salomon loquitur : Via stulti recta in oculis ejus. Hinc omnis peccans dicitur esse ignorans, quia erronee judicat, saltem in particulari. Unde et in Habacuc habetur : Quomodo vinum potantem decipit, sic erit vir superbus. Et luxurioso presbytero Daniel dixit : Species decepit te.
paras.en: The holy apostle James has now admonished us that, all uncleanness and malice being rooted out, we should receive with meekness the ingrafted word of God. But lest we should think it enough for us to hear the word of God, he now adds: [[1:22|But be ye doers of the word and not hearers only|Estote autem factores verbi, et non auditores tantum]]: that is, do not only hear the sayings of the commandments of God and of the Church, but also fulfil them in deed. So too Paul taught: [[Rom 2:13|not the hearers of the law are just before God: but the doers of the law shall be justified|Non auditores legis justi sunt apud Deum, sed factores legis justificabuntur]]; and the Prophet: [[Ps 110:10|A good understanding to all that do it|Intellectus bonus omnibus facientibus eum]]. For moral knowledge is ordered to action. Wherefore the Philosopher said: We inquire what virtue is, not that we may know it, but that we may become good. And again, in the first book of the Ethics, he testifies that those who attend to moral instruction but do not carry it out in deed are like sick men who listen carefully to their physicians but do not keep to their teaching. So then, [[1:22|be ye doers of the word and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves|Estote factores verbi, non auditores tantum, fallentes vosmetipsos]]: for those who are content with hearing alone deceive themselves: either formally and directly, as when they think it enough for their salvation only to hear and to know; or concomitantly, that is, equivalently or materially, in the sense that everyone who sins deceives himself, according to that saying, [[Prov 14:9|A fool will laugh at sin|Stultus illudit peccatum]] [Latin *illudit*, "mocks", also means "deludes": Denis takes the verse to mean that sin deludes the fool]. And again Solomon says: [[Prov 12:15|The way of a fool is right in his own eyes|Via stulti recta in oculis ejus]]. Hence every sinner is said to be ignorant, because he judges wrongly, at least in the particular case. Whence also we have in Habacuc: [[Hab 2:5|as wine deceiveth him that drinketh it: so shall the proud man be|Quomodo vinum potantem decipit, sic erit vir superbus]]. And Daniel said to the lustful elder: [[Dan 13:56|beauty hath deceived thee|Species decepit te]].

paras.t: Quia si quis auditor est verbi, et non factor, hic comparabitur viro consideranti vultum nativitatis suæ, id est faciem suam corporalem cum qua natus est, in speculo. Consideravit enim se, id est dispositionem vultus sui, et abiit, et statim oblitus est qualis fuerit, id est, distinctam suæ dispositionis notitiam mox amisit, nec perfectam suæ physionomiæ servavit memoriam. Cujus ratio assignatur, quia imago in speculo habet debile esse, et intentionale potius quam reale, ut dicitur. Ideo debilem facit impressionem, quia modus agendi sequitur modum essendi. Et quia debilem facit impressionem in oculo, ex tali impressione sequitur labilis in mente cognitio. Conformiter, qui verba Dei audit, nec implet, imperfectam et informem habet eorum memoriam, aut penitus nullam.
paras.en: [[1:23|For if a man be a hearer of the word and not a doer|Quia si quis auditor est verbi, et non factor]], [[1:23|he shall be compared to a man beholding his own countenance|hic comparabitur viro consideranti vultum nativitatis suæ]] [literally "the countenance of his birth"], that is, his bodily face, with which he was born, [[1:23|in a glass|in speculo]]. [[1:24|For he beheld himself|Consideravit enim se]], that is, the cast of his face, [[1:24|and went his way and presently forgot what manner of man he was|et abiit, et statim oblitus est qualis fuerit]], that is, he soon lost the distinct knowledge of how he looked, and kept no perfect memory of his features. The reason for this is given: that an image in a mirror has a weak being, intentional rather than real, as it is said [*intentional* being: the being a thing has as an object of sight or thought, as opposed to its real being in itself]. Therefore it makes a weak impression, because the manner of acting follows the manner of being. And because it makes a weak impression on the eye, from such an impression there follows a fleeting knowledge in the mind. In like manner, he who hears the words of God and does not fulfil them has an imperfect and unformed memory of them, or none at all.

paras.t: Qui autem perspexerit, id est, perspicaciter consideraverit, in lege perfecta (seu, ut alii legunt, perfectæ libertatis), ea quæ scribuntur, docentur, et præcipiuntur in ea, puta in Evangelio. Denique, sive legatur, Perfecta, sive, Perfectæ, verus est sensus. — Lex enim evangelica, respectu legis Moysis, est perfecta, et excellentias multas sortitur, prout in Prologo super Lucam diffuse ostensum est; et ipsa ceteras universas in perfectione superat leges. Dicitur quoque lex evangelica, lex libertatis perfectæ : Primo, quia per eam exoneramur ab obligatione observantiæ veteris legis. Propter quod sacratissimus apostolici ordinis princeps, gloriosissimus Petrus, ait : Quid tentatis Deum, imponere jugum super cervices discipulorum, quod neque patres nostri, neque nos portare potuimus? Sed per gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi credimus salvari. Et Paulus apostolus : Lex spiritus vitæ in Christo Jesu, liberavit me a lege peccati et mortis. Et rursus clarius loquens : Nunc sine lege justitia Dei manifestata est per fidem Jesu Christi, in omnes et super omnes qui credunt in eum. — Secundo, quia lex evangelica est lex caritatis et gratiæ; lex vetus fuit lex timoris et pœnæ. Idcirco, secundum Augustinum, brevis differentia Evangelii et legis, est amor et timor. Lex quippe evangelica dicitur lex amoris et gratiæ, in quantum continet salutifera sacramenta gratiæ continentiva, et quia in Evangelio præclarissime describuntur amor et pietas Dei ad homines, et beneficia ac promissa ipsius. Inducit quoque lex ista ad sui observantiam potius per amorem et præmii pollicitationem, quam per terrorem et comminationem pœnarum. Porro lex vetus dicitur lex timoris, quia nec gratiam continebat, et transgressoribus suis etiam temporalem mortem mox infligi præcepit : et ita quasi quadam coactione atque formidine, ad sui observationem induxit. Propter quod ad Hebræos fertur : Irritam quis faciens legem Moysis, absque ulla contradictione duobus aut tribus testibus moritur. Lex autem evangelica transgressoribus suis pœnitentiam consulit, veniamque promittit. Hinc dicit Apostolus : Nihil ad perfectum adduxit lex (quia videlicet ejus sacramenta non erant gratiæ contentiva) : itemque, Non dedit nobis Deus spiritum timoris, sed spiritum virtutis et dilectionis et sobrietatis. — Tertio, quia per evangelicæ legis observationem liberamur ab omni jugo diaboli et servitute peccati, quemadmodum Paulus : Per Jesum, inquit, remissio vobis peccatorum annuntiatur, ab omnibus a quibus non potuistis in lege Moysis justificari. — Quarto, quia per evangelicæ legis impletionem, ad æternam felicitatem, in qua est cœlestis ac plena libertas, indilate perducimur : quod per Mosaicæ legis observantiam non fiebat. Hinc Unigenitus Patris ait : Si Filius vos liberaverit, vere liberi eritis. Huic autem libertati non repugnat servitus caritatis, quum Deo servire sit regnare. Atque ut devotissima Agatha dixit, Summa ingenuitas est, in qua Christi servitus comprobatur. Ideo Paulus disseruit : Ubi spiritus Domini, ibi libertas.
paras.en: [[1:25|But he that hath looked into|Qui autem perspexerit]], that is, has looked closely, [[1:25|the perfect law|in lege perfecta]] (or, as others read, *of perfect liberty* [Latin *perfectæ libertatis*, so that the whole reads "into the law of perfect liberty"]): into the things that are written, taught and commanded in it, that is, in the Gospel. In short, whether one reads *perfect* or *of perfect*, the sense is true. For the law of the Gospel, compared with the law of Moses, is perfect, and has been given many excellences, as was shown at length in the Prologue on Luke; and it surpasses all other laws whatever in perfection. The law of the Gospel is also called the law of perfect liberty. First, because by it we are released from the obligation of keeping the old law. Wherefore the most holy prince of the apostolic order, the most glorious Peter, says: [[Acts 15:10|why tempt you God to put a yoke upon the necks of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?|Quid tentatis Deum, imponere jugum super cervices discipulorum, quod neque patres nostri, neque nos portare potuimus?]]? [[Acts 15:11|But by the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, we believe to be saved|Sed per gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi credimus salvari]]. And Paul the apostle: [[Rom 8:2|the law of the spirit of life, in Christ Jesus, hath delivered me from the law of sin and of death|Lex spiritus vitæ in Christo Jesu, liberavit me a lege peccati et mortis]] [the margin gives Rom. vii, 2; the words are Rom 8:2]. And again, speaking more clearly: [[Rom 3:21|now, without the law, the justice of God is made manifest|Nunc sine lege justitia Dei manifestata est]] [[Rom 3:22|by faith of Jesus Christ, unto all, and upon all them that believe in him|per fidem Jesu Christi, in omnes et super omnes qui credunt in eum]]. Secondly, because the law of the Gospel is the law of charity and grace; the old law was a law of fear and punishment. Therefore, according to Augustine, the difference between the Gospel and the law, in brief, is love and fear. For the law of the Gospel is called the law of love and grace inasmuch as it contains the saving sacraments that contain grace, and because in the Gospel the love and kindness of God towards men, and his benefits and promises, are most clearly set forth. This law also leads men to keep it by love and the promise of reward rather than by terror and the threat of punishment. But the old law is called the law of fear, because it did not contain grace, and it commanded that even temporal death be inflicted at once on its transgressors: and so it led men to keep it as it were by a certain compulsion and dread. Wherefore it is said to the Hebrews: [[Heb 10:28|A man making void the law of Moses|Irritam quis faciens legem Moysis]] dies without any gainsaying [Denis reads *absque ulla contradictione*, "without any gainsaying", where the Vulgate has *sine ulla miseratione*, "without any mercy"] [[Heb 10:28|under two or three witnesses|duobus aut tribus testibus]]. But the law of the Gospel counsels penance to its transgressors and promises them pardon. Hence the Apostle says: [[Heb 7:19|the law brought nothing to perfection|Nihil ad perfectum adduxit lex]] (because, that is, its sacraments did not contain grace); and likewise, [[2 Tim 1:7|God hath not given us the spirit of fear|Non dedit nobis Deus spiritum timoris]], [[2 Tim 1:7|but of power and of love and of sobriety|sed spiritum virtutis et dilectionis et sobrietatis]]. Thirdly, because by keeping the law of the Gospel we are set free from every yoke of the devil and from the servitude of sin, as Paul says: Through Jesus, he says, [[Acts 13:38|forgiveness of sins is preached to you|remissio vobis peccatorum annuntiatur]], [[Acts 13:38|from all the things from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses|ab omnibus a quibus non potuistis in lege Moysis justificari]]. Fourthly, because by fulfilling the law of the Gospel we are brought without delay to eternal happiness, in which is heavenly and full liberty: which did not come about through keeping the Mosaic law. Hence the Only-begotten of the Father says: [[John 8:36|If therefore the son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed|Si Filius vos liberaverit, vere liberi eritis]]. Now the service of charity is not opposed to this liberty, since to serve God is to reign. And, as the most devout Agatha said, the highest nobility [Latin *ingenuitas*, the standing of one born free] is that in which the service of Christ is shown. Therefore Paul taught: [[2 Cor 3:17|where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty|Ubi spiritus Domini, ibi libertas]].

paras.t: Itaque qui in hac lege perspexerit, et permanserit in ea, fide et opere stabilis : quoniam sola perseverantia coronatur, Christo dicente, Qui perseveraverit usque in finem, hic salvus erit; non auditor obliviosus factus, id est verba salutis oblivioni non tradens, sed factor operis, id est exsecutor operum quæ Deus præcepit : hic beatus in facto suo erit, id est, per opera sua beatitudinem obtinebit : sicut in Evangelio Dominus contestatur, Si vis intrare ad vitam, serva mandata; et denuo, Si hæc scitis, beati eritis si feceritis ea. Etenim omnis arbor quæ non fecerit fructum bonum, excidetur, et in ignem mittetur. Præterea, dupliciter dicitur homo divinorum oblivisci verborum : primo, ea a sua memoria penitus amittendo; secundo, ea non adimplendo. Nam et invariabilis Deus dicitur oblivisci eorum quos justo judicio perire permittit, eo quod per modum oblivisciens circa illos se habeat. Unde Threnorum ultimo dicitur : Quare in perpetuum oblivisceris nostri?
paras.en: So then he who has looked into this law [[1:25|and hath continued therein|et permanserit in ea]], steadfast in faith and in deed (since perseverance alone is crowned, as Christ says, [[Matt 24:13|he that shall persevere to the end, he shall be saved|Qui perseveraverit usque in finem, hic salvus erit]]); [[1:25|not becoming a forgetful hearer|non auditor obliviosus factus]], that is, not giving over the words of salvation to forgetfulness, [[1:25|but a doer of the work|sed factor operis]], that is, one who carries out the works that God has commanded: [[1:25|this man shall be blessed in his deed|hic beatus in facto suo erit]], that is, by his works he will obtain beatitude; as the Lord testifies in the Gospel, [[Matt 19:17|if thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments|Si vis intrare ad vitam, serva mandata]]; and again, [[John 13:17|If you know these things, you shall be blessed if you do them|Si hæc scitis, beati eritis si feceritis ea]]. For [[Matt 7:19|Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit, shall be cut down, and shall be cast into the fire|omnis arbor quæ non fecerit fructum bonum, excidetur, et in ignem mittetur]]. Moreover, a man is said to forget the divine words in two ways: first, by losing them wholly from his memory; secondly, by not fulfilling them. For even the unchangeable God is said to forget those whom by just judgment he allows to perish, in that he deals with them in the manner of one who forgets. Whence it is said in the last chapter of Lamentations: [[Lam 5:20|Why wilt thou forget us for ever|Quare in perpetuum oblivisceris nostri]]?

paras.t: Postquam apostolus Jacobus docuit, non sufficere ad salutem verba Dei audire, sed oportere ea operibus exercere, nunc ostendit nec hoc sufficere, nisi et peccata locutionis vitentur. Hinc subditur : Si quis autem putat se religiosum esse, id est verum christianæ fidei professorem, ac latriæ servatorem, atque devotum, non refrenans linguam suam a multiloquio, detractione, mendacio, ac ceteris verbis prohibitis, sed seducens cor suum, id est a recto salutis itinere illud avertens, et per incustodiam, negligentiam, errores et vitia, se ipsum fallens atque obtenebrans, quemadmodum per Osee Dominus ait : Ephraim quasi columba seducta, non habens cor; hujus vana est religio, id est, frustra se Christianum esse fatetur, nec est in eo veraciter latria sive devotio, sed ficte aut apparenter dumtaxat. De talibus fertur in Osee : Ventum seminabunt, et turbinem metent.
paras.en: After the apostle James has taught that it is not enough for salvation to hear the words of God, but that one must put them into practice in works, he now shows that not even this is enough unless sins of speech are also avoided. Hence it follows: [[1:26|And if any man think himself to be religious|Si quis autem putat se religiosum esse]], that is, a true professor of the Christian faith, a keeper of latria [the worship due to God alone], and devout, [[1:26|not bridling his tongue|non refrenans linguam suam]] from much speaking, detraction, lying and other forbidden words, [[1:26|but deceiving his own heart|sed seducens cor suum]], that is, turning it away from the right road of salvation, and through want of watchfulness, through negligence, errors and vices, deceiving and darkening himself; as the Lord says through Osee: [[Osee 7:11|Ephraim is become as a dove that is decoyed, not having a heart|Ephraim quasi columba seducta, non habens cor]] [the margin gives Osee viii, 11; the words are Osee 7:11. *Seducta*, "decoyed", is the same word as *seducens*, "deceiving", in the verse]; [[1:26|this man's religion is vain|hujus vana est religio]], that is, he professes himself a Christian in vain, and there is in him no true latria or devotion, but only a feigned or apparent one. Of such it is said in Osee: [[Osee 8:7|they shall sow wind, and reap a whirlwind|Ventum seminabunt, et turbinem metent]].

paras.t: Quum ergo illa sit vana religio, docet quid sit vera religio. Religio munda et immaculata, id est intus et foris sincera, coram Deo et hominibus approbata, in se ipsa et in suis operibus pura, apud Deum et Patrem, id est coram Deo, qui est omnium Deus et pater; vel, Coram Deo Filio et Patre æterno, qui cum Spiritu Sancto sunt unus omnium Deus, unus creator, et unus finis; hæc est : Visitare pupillos et viduas in tribulatione eorum, id est opera misericordiæ proximis impertire, præsertim miserabilibus personis, humano solatio destitutis (ut sunt pupilli et orphani, viduæ, peregrini, oppressi, tentati, infirmi, captivi, mendici, pauperesque domestici) subvenire, et eos corporaliter visitare ac consolari. Beati enim misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur. Et Christus in die judicii dicet : Quod uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis. Hinc in Ecclesiastico dicitur : Non desis plorantibus in consolatione; et non te pigeat visitare infirmum : ex his enim in dilectione firmaberis. In Job quoque : Visitans speciem tuam, non peccabis, id est proximos et egenos, qui ejusdem tecum sunt speciei. De quibus loquitur Isaias : Frange esurienti panem tuum, et egenos vagosque induc in domum tuam; quum videris nudum, operi eum. Et immaculatum se custodire ab hoc sæculo, id est vanitates et impietates, atque illicitas voluptates mundanorum hominum devitare, juxta illud : Nolite conformari huic sæculo, sed reformamini in novitate sensus vestri. Unde alibi ait Apostolus : Qui utuntur hoc mundo, sint tanquam non utentes. Nam, ut Joannes ait apostolus, Omne quod est in mundo, concupiscentia carnis est, et concupiscentia oculorum, et superbia vitæ.
paras.en: Since, then, that religion is vain, he teaches what true religion is. [[1:27|Religion clean and undefiled|Religio munda et immaculata]], that is, sincere within and without, approved before God and men, pure in itself and in its works, [[1:27|before God and the Father|apud Deum et Patrem]], that is, before God, who is the God and Father of all; or, before God the Son and the eternal Father, who with the Holy Ghost are the one God of all, one creator and one end, [[1:27|is this: to visit the fatherless and widows in their tribulation|hæc est : Visitare pupillos et viduas in tribulatione eorum]]: that is, to bestow works of mercy on one's neighbours; above all, to succour wretched persons, bereft of human comfort (such as wards and orphans, widows, strangers, the oppressed, the tempted, the sick, captives, beggars, and the poor at home), and to visit and console them in person. For [[Matt 5:7|Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy|Beati enim misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur]]. And Christ will say on the day of judgment: [[Matt 25:40|as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me|Quod uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis]]. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 7:38|Be not wanting in comforting them that weep|Non desis plorantibus in consolatione]]; and [[Ecclus 7:39|Be not slow to visit the sick: for by these things thou shalt be confirmed in love|non te pigeat visitare infirmum : ex his enim in dilectione firmaberis]]. In Job too: [[Job 5:24|visiting thy beauty, thou shalt not sin|Visitans speciem tuam, non peccabis]], that is, thy neighbours and the needy, who are of the same kind [*speciei*] as thou [Latin *species* means both "beauty" and "kind": Denis takes it in the second sense]. Of whom Isaias speaks: [[Is 58:7|Deal thy bread to the hungry, and bring the needy and the harbourless into thy house: when thou shalt see one naked, cover him|Frange esurienti panem tuum, et egenos vagosque induc in domum tuam; quum videris nudum, operi eum]]. [[1:27|and to keep one's self unspotted from this world|Et immaculatum se custodire ab hoc sæculo]]: that is, to shun the vanities and impieties and the unlawful pleasures of worldly men, according to that saying: [[Rom 12:2|be not conformed to this world: but be reformed in the newness of your mind|Nolite conformari huic sæculo, sed reformamini in novitate sensus vestri]]. Whence the Apostle says elsewhere: [[1 Cor 7:31|they that use this world, as if they used it not|Qui utuntur hoc mundo, sint tanquam non utentes]]. For, as John the apostle says, [[1 John 2:16|all that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh and the concupiscence of the eyes and the pride of life|Omne quod est in mundo, concupiscentia carnis est, et concupiscentia oculorum, et superbia vitæ]].

paras.t: Circa præhabita, quærenda sunt aliqua : Primo, quid sit religio, et de actibus ejus, qui etiam sint vere religiosi; deinde de refrenatione linguæ, præsertim quantum ad claustrales; postremo, quid sit, se immaculatum ab hoc sæculo custodire. De horum primo dicit hoc loco Albertus : Religiosus idem designat quod religatus. Sed religatio ista potest attendi tripliciter : Primo, penes observationem præceptorum articulorumque fidei : sicque omnes veraciter christiani sunt religiosi. Secundo, penes observationem evangelicorum consiliorum : et sic claustrales cœnobitæ religiosi vocantur. Tertio, penes custodiam oris : et sic qui linguam suam ab illicitis cohibet verbis, dicitur proprie religiosus. Verum de ista materia multo plenius scribit Thomas in secunda secundæ, dicendo : Religio dicitur a relegendo, quoniam quæ ad divinum pertinent cultum, sæpe sunt relegenda ac revolvenda, juxta illud : Quæ præcepit tibi Deus, illa cogita semper. Vel dicitur religio a reeligendo, quoniam Deum quem peccando amisimus, et cui vana prætulimus, per eam pœnitentes reeligimus; vel a religando, quia ab exterioribus et carnalibus hominem separat, ac Deo conjungit. Itaque religio est virtus moralis, quæ alio nomine latria appellatur, per quam Deo cultum cæremoniamque impendimus. Nec est theologica virtus, sed pars subjectiva justitiæ, circa actiones immediate versans : habetque aliquos actus interiores, ut sunt devotio interna, oratio; et quosdam actus exteriores, ut sunt Deo genua flectere, sacrificare, immolare. Vocalis quoque oratio, psalmodia, laudatio Dei, prædicare verbum salutis, sunt actus religionis, quasi medio modo se habentes. Et omnia ista sunt actus religionis, directe et elicitive, quia ab ea elicitive procedunt. Actus vero quarumdam virtutum religione inferiorum, quibus religio imperat, dicuntur actus ejus imperative, quia imperat eos. Sicque præfata misericordiæ opera religioni attribuuntur, quæ tamen a pietate seu misericordia eliciuntur.
paras.en: On what has been said, some questions are to be asked: first, what religion is, and of its acts, and also who are truly religious; then, of the bridling of the tongue, especially as regards those in the cloister; lastly, what it is [[1:27|to keep one's self unspotted from this world|se immaculatum ab hoc sæculo custodire]]. On the first of these Albert says in this place: *Religious* means the same as *bound back* [Latin *religatus*]. But this binding can be considered in three ways. First, as to the keeping of the commandments and of the articles of faith: and so all who are truly Christians are religious. Secondly, as to the keeping of the evangelical counsels: and so cenobites in the cloister are called religious. Thirdly, as to the guarding of the mouth: and so he who holds his tongue back from unlawful words is properly called religious. But Thomas writes much more fully on this matter in the Secunda Secundae, saying: Religion is named from *reading again* [*relegere*], because the things that belong to divine worship must often be read again and turned over, according to that saying: [[Ecclus 3:22|the things that God hath commanded thee, think on them always|Quæ præcepit tibi Deus, illa cogita semper]]. Or religion is named from *choosing again* [*reeligere*], because by it, as penitents, we choose again God, whom we lost by sinning and before whom we set vain things; or from *binding back* [*religare*], because it parts man from outward and carnal things and joins him to God. Religion, then, is a moral virtue, which by another name is called latria, by which we render worship and ceremony to God. Nor is it a theological virtue, but a subjective part of justice [that is, one of the species into which justice is divided], dealing immediately with actions; and it has certain interior acts, such as inward devotion and prayer, and certain exterior acts, such as bending the knee to God, offering sacrifice, immolating. Vocal prayer also, psalmody, the praise of God, preaching the word of salvation, are acts of religion, holding as it were a middle place. And all these are acts of religion directly and elicitively, because they proceed from it as from the virtue that elicits them. But the acts of certain virtues lower than religion, which religion commands, are called its acts imperatively, because it commands them [an act is *elicited* by the virtue that itself produces it, and *commanded* by a higher virtue that directs it to its own end]. And so the works of mercy mentioned above are attributed to religion, though they are elicited by piety or mercy.

paras.t: Præterea, refrenatio linguæ ad omnem pertinet Christianum, quum in Evangelio Christus testetur : De omni verbo otioso quod locuti fuerint homines, reddent de eo rationem in die judicii; itemque, Ex ore tuo justificaberis, et ex ore tuo condemnaberis; et iterum, Quæ procedunt de ore, coinquinant hominem. Denique, quam necessaria sit omni homini refrenatio linguæ, constat ex eo quod ait Judex summus : Qui dixerit fratri suo, Raca, reus erit concilio; qui autem dixerit, Fatue, reus erit gehennæ ignis. Præterea, quia claustrales antonomastice religiosi dicuntur, utpote Deo in holocaustum oblati, ejusque cultui totaliter mancipati, hinc ad eos refrenatio linguæ potissimum pertinet. Propter quod sancti Patres, inter regulares observantias observationem silentii, unam de præcipuis post substantialia statuerunt, et ejus fractionem per culpæ publicationem, proclamationem ac disciplinam vindicari seu corrigi præceperunt. Hinc omnis oratio intelligibilem ex se habens sensum, sine licentia prolata, nisi necessitas sit excusans, est silentii fractio, ut si dicatur, Quis est iste? Attendant hæc religiosi remissi, intimorati, leves, incustoditi et garruli. Attendant quam sit vana eorum, quam prætendunt, religio. Advertant quod ait Psalmista : Vir linguosus non dirigetur in terra; et quod rursus ait Scriptura, Numquid vir verbosus justificabitur? Imo, juxta Scripturam, verba sapientis statera ponderabuntur. Non ergo verbis pereffluamus, quia odibilis est, qui procax est ad loquendum. Hinc Ecclesiastes : Ne temere quid loquaris, neque cor tuum sit velox ad proferendum sermonem coram Deo. Deus enim in cœlo, et tu super terram : idcirco sint pauci sermones tui. In multis namque sermonibus invenitur stultitia.
paras.en: Moreover, the bridling of the tongue belongs to every Christian, since Christ testifies in the Gospel: [[Matt 12:36|every idle word that men shall speak, they shall render an account for it in the day of judgment|De omni verbo otioso quod locuti fuerint homines, reddent de eo rationem in die judicii]]; and likewise, [[Matt 12:37|by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned|Ex ore tuo justificaberis, et ex ore tuo condemnaberis]] [Denis reads *ex ore tuo*, "by thy mouth", where the Vulgate has *ex verbis tuis*, "by thy words"]; and again, [[Matt 15:18|the things which proceed out of the mouth|Quæ procedunt de ore]] [[Matt 15:18|defile a man|coinquinant hominem]] [the margin gives Ibid. xii, 37 here as well; the words are Matt 15:18, cf. 15:11]. Finally, how necessary the bridling of the tongue is for every man is plain from what the supreme Judge says: [[Matt 5:22|whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council. And whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire|Qui dixerit fratri suo, Raca, reus erit concilio; qui autem dixerit, Fatue, reus erit gehennæ ignis]]. Moreover, because those in the cloister are called religious by antonomasia [that is, the common name is given to them as its chief bearers], as men offered to God as a holocaust and wholly given over to his worship, the bridling of the tongue belongs to them above all. Wherefore the holy Fathers, among the regular observances, established the keeping of silence as one of the chief after the substantial ones [that is, after the vows that are of the substance of religious life], and ordered that the breaking of it be punished or corrected by the publishing of the fault, by proclamation [the accusing of a brother's fault in chapter] and by discipline. Hence every utterance that has of itself an intelligible sense, spoken without leave, unless necessity excuses it, is a breach of silence: as if one should say, Who is that? Let slack religious heed these things, the fearless, the light, the unguarded and the garrulous. Let them heed how vain is the religion they make a show of. Let them mark what the Psalmist says: [[Ps 139:12|A man full of tongue shall not be established in the earth|Vir linguosus non dirigetur in terra]]; and what Scripture says again: [[Job 11:2|shall a man full of talk be justified|Numquid vir verbosus justificabitur?]]? Nay rather, according to Scripture, [[Ecclus 21:28|the words of the wise shall be weighed in a balance|verba sapientis statera ponderabuntur]]. Let us not then overflow with words, for he [[Ecclus 20:5|is hateful, that is bold in speech|odibilis est, qui procax est ad loquendum]]. Hence Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 5:1|Speak not any thing rashly, and let not thy heart be hasty to utter a word before God. For God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few|Ne temere quid loquaris, neque cor tuum sit velox ad proferendum sermonem coram Deo. Deus enim in cœlo, et tu super terram : idcirco sint pauci sermones tui]]. For [[Eccles 5:2|in many words shall be found folly|In multis namque sermonibus invenitur stultitia]] [the margin notes beside these four quotations from Ps, Job and Ecclus are unreadable in the transcription; the references are supplied from the words].

paras.t: Verumtamen circa hoc quæritur, quomodo in verbis sit paucitas observanda, quum in Actibus Apostolorum legatur Paulus protraxisse sermonem usque ad mediam noctem, et exhortatus discipulos multo sermone. Christus quoque in monte fecit longum sermonem. Ecclesia etiam facit orationes prolixas, quum tamen etiam dicat Salvator : Orantes nolite multum loqui. Et respondendum, quod Scripturæ intentio est, ut non sine rationabili causa verba multiplicentur, propter periculum incidendi peccata : quod in verbis multis sine gratia vix cavetur. Christus vero non prohibuit absolute uti multis verbis in oratione, quum et ipse passione instante, prolixius orasse legatur, et quod erat pernoctans in oratione Dei. Sed dixit : Orantes nolite multum loqui, sicut ethnici faciunt : putant enim quod in multiloquio suo exaudiantur. — Sit ergo religiosus in observatione silentii rigorosus. Qui enim custodit os suum, custodit ab angustiis animam suam; qui vero inconsideratus est ad loquendum, sentiet mala.
paras.en: Yet on this point it is asked how fewness of words is to be kept, since in the Acts of the Apostles we read that Paul [[Acts 20:7|continued his speech until midnight|protraxisse sermonem usque ad mediam noctem]], and exhorted the disciples with many words [cf. Acts 20:2]. Christ too made a long sermon on the mountain[[Matt 5:1||]] [the margin gives Matth. v, with the verse unreadable]. The Church also makes long prayers, though the Saviour also says: [[Matt 6:7|when you are praying, speak not much|Orantes nolite multum loqui]]. And the answer is that the intention of Scripture is that words should not be multiplied without reasonable cause, because of the danger of falling into sins, which among many words is hardly avoided without grace. But Christ did not absolutely forbid the use of many words in prayer, since he himself, when his passion was at hand, is read to have prayed the longer[[Luke 22:43||]] [the margin note here is unreadable in the transcription], and that he [[Luke 6:12|passed the whole night in the prayer of God|erat pernoctans in oratione Dei]] [the margin gives Ibid. vi, 12: the passage is Luke 6:12]. But he said: [[Matt 6:7|when you are praying, speak not much, as the heathens. For they think that in their much speaking they may be heard|Orantes nolite multum loqui, sicut ethnici faciunt : putant enim quod in multiloquio suo exaudiantur]]. Let the religious, then, be strict in keeping silence. For [[Prov 21:23|He that keepeth his mouth|custodit os suum]] [[Prov 21:23|keepeth his soul from distress|custodit ab angustiis animam suam]]; but [[Prov 13:3|he that hath no guard on his speech shall meet with evils|qui vero inconsideratus est ad loquendum, sentiet mala]] [the margin notes beside these two quotations are unreadable in the transcription; the references are supplied from the words].

paras.t: Postremo, immaculatum se ab hoc sæculo custodire, est ad nullam rem creatam affici inordinate; divitias, delicias et honores mundi, intuitu et amore Dei parvi pendere, aut omnino relinquere; nec aliquid citra Deum, nisi in Deo amare, hoc est, in quantum Deus id præcipit, seu utile necessariumve exsistit ad complacendum serviendumque Deo, atque ad obtinendum beatificam fruitionem ipsius. Quum enim Deus gloriosus et adorandus, sit omnium finis, et media juxta exigentiam finis sint disponenda : certum est quod nulla res creata sit appetenda, amanda, servanda, tractanda, aut quocumque modo in usu habenda, nisi secundum quod expedit homini ad uniendum se Deo, atque ad obtinendum ipsius visionem felicem, seu ad serviendum ei, et ad proficiendum in cultu ac honorificentia ejus. Quod totum ad religiosos maxime spectat, quos oportet esse huic sæculo mortuos, et soli Deo viventes, ut cum Apostolo dicere queant : Vivo autem, jam non ego; vivit vero in me Christus.
paras.en: Lastly, [[1:27|to keep one's self unspotted from this world|immaculatum se ab hoc sæculo custodire]] is to be inordinately attached to no created thing; to think little of the riches, delights and honours of the world, or to leave them altogether, out of regard for God and love of him; and to love nothing short of God except in God: that is, inasmuch as God commands it, or it is useful or necessary for pleasing and serving God and for obtaining the beatific enjoyment of him. For since the glorious and adorable God is the end of all things, and the means are to be ordered as the end requires, it is certain that no created thing is to be desired, loved, kept, handled, or in any way had in use, except so far as it helps man to unite himself to God and to obtain the happy vision of him, or to serve him and to advance in his worship and honour. All of which concerns religious most of all, who must be dead to this world and live to God alone, so that they can say with the Apostle: [[Gal 2:20|And I live, now not I: but Christ liveth in me|Vivo autem, jam non ego; vivit vero in me Christus]].
